speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister, Coordinating Minister for National Security and Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Road accidents, which can lead to severe and irreversible consequences for victims and their families are entirely preventable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our accident rates and fatality numbers need to come down.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Last year we had a record high of 149 fatalities – almost one death every two days on the roads.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There are several pillars in our approach towards promoting road safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: One pillar is having strong and effective laws.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Over the years, the Ministry has reviewed and updated the Road Traffic Act (RTA) to ensure that it remains fit-for-purpose.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Since 2019, the Act has been amended four times.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We seek to do so again today, to achieve three key objectives: First, strengthen accountability for the most egregious road conduct; Second, further deter driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs; and third, enhance the Traffic Police's ability to detect and enforce against traffic offences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will amend the RTA in two ways to ensure this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Members may recall the case of Jarrett Tee.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Whilst racing a motorcyclist along a highway, the offender deliberately swerved his car to cut off the motorcycle and prior to doing so, said to his passengers, "Do you want to see motorcycle fly?" The offender's car then side-swiped the motorcycle, causing the motorcyclist and the pillion passenger to be flung off the motorcycle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The pillion rider passed away as a result.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Prosecution described the case as, "One of the worst examples of dangerous driving possible," and his culpability was, "on the extreme end of high".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Yet the most serious charge that the offender could face, based on the facts of the case, was dangerous driving causing death, which carries a maximum imprisonment sentence of eight years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Government's view is that such conduct must face harsher consequences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Where an offender deliberately uses a vehicle to endanger another person's life or safety, for example, by deliberately swerving a motor vehicle towards another driver to force the latter off the road or purposefully driving one's vehicle towards another road user, the offender's culpability is significantly higher than that of a driver who speeds or beats a red light.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, existing RTA offences do not adequately distinguish purposeful endangerment from dangerous driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It may also be challenging for the Prosecution to prove that the conduct fulfilled the mental elements required for more serious Penal Code offences, such as murder, culpable homicide or voluntarily causing grievous hurt by dangerous means.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For example, in a case like Jarrett Tee, where a driver deliberately swerves to cut off the motorcycle, it may be difficult to prove that he did so with the knowledge that death or grievous hurt was likely to result.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clause 6, therefore, introduces a new offence of purposeful endangerment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It fills a gap in respect of offenders who deliberately use their vehicle to endanger another person's life or safety.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Given the severity of the conduct, the penalties for the offence will be higher than those for dangerous driving causing death.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Court must also impose driving disqualification for life, unless there are special reasons not to do so; and if special reasons apply, the Court must impose at least 10 years of driving disqualification.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Court may also order the forfeiture of the vehicle used in the commission of the offence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The offence will apply even if the person who died or suffered grievous hurt is not the person whom the offender intended to endanger.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This ensures that the offender remains fully accountable for the consequences of their conduct.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Second, the Bill raises the penalties for careless and dangerous driving causing grievous hurt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are making this amendment because the most serious forms of grievous hurt may cause victims to suffer permanent, life-altering consequences, leaving them unable to work, live independently or care for themselves.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For example, Members may recall a recent case of an auxiliary police officer who was on duty at Tuas Checkpoint when a drunk driver collided into him.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: He survived the collision but suffered traumatic brain injuries and is now paralysed and requires lifelong care.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The penalties in such cases must be proportionate to the harm.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Yet today, the maximum penalties for reckless or dangerous driving, which I will hereafter refer to as dangerous driving, causing grievous hurt under the RTA remain significantly lower than those causing death.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clause 7, therefore, increases the maximum penalties for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt, bringing them closer to the corresponding offences causing death.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Clauses 7 and 8 of the Bill also increases the additional imprisonment terms that serious offenders are liable for.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Serious offenders referring to those who drove under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our intention is for the increased penalty range to only apply to the most egregious cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We do not intend to affect the prevailing sentencing benchmarks for those with lower culpability or who cause less serious forms of grievous hurt.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Ministry will work with the Sentencing Advisory Panel to develop sentencing guidelines to give effect to this intent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It poses a serious threat to the safety of all road users.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Every instance of driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs is entirely preventable and highly culpable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Yet year after year, we continue to see far too many motorists make this dangerous decision.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Over the past five years, the Traffic Police detected between 1,500 and 1,800 drink-driving violations annually.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: And we know this is an under-detection, because drink driving generally can only be detected at roadblocks and with our limited operational resources, we cannot be setting up roadblocks everywhere.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This Bill introduces two provisions to enhance deterrence against driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The current prescribed alcohol limits have been in force since 1985.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Since then, scientific understanding of alcohol impairment has advanced considerably.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Many jurisdictions, including Thailand, Philippines, Australia and South Korea have adopted lower prescribed alcohol limits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The evidence today consistently shows that even low levels of alcohol can impair a driver's reaction time, judgement, concentration and ability to respond safely to situations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As blood alcohol concentration increases, the degree of impairment increases and so does the risk posed to other road users.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The new prescribed limits represent the point at which impairment and thus, unacceptable risk to road users begins.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The new prescribed limits broadly correspond to no more than 1.5 standard drinks for males and not more than one standard drink for females, consumed three hours before driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These are only broad illustrations for reference and do not represent the "safe" number of drinks to go below the revised limits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is because the effects of alcohol differ significantly depending on factors, such as age, sex, health and body composition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our message remains: if you drink, do not drive.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: You cannot be sure of your level of impairment after drinking, so do not take the risk.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As we make this amendment, the sentencing guidelines applicable to the new alcohol limits would also need to be reviewed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Ministry's view is that offenders who drive with very high blood alcohol levels should face imprisonment given the significant risks such conduct poses to other road users and to enhance deterrence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will work with the Sentencing Advisory Panel to consider issuing new sentencing guidelines for drink driving, including guidelines on when imprisonment is warranted.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I refer to these substances collectively as "specified substances".

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Today, it is already an offence to drive under the influence of specified substances in a manner that results in impaired driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, while it is an offence to drive simply with a certain concentration of alcohol in one's blood, there is no corresponding offence for specified substances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is because there is no single scientifically established concentration threshold that can reliably indicate impairment across a wide range of such substances.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Instead, under the current offence, the prosecution must prove not only that the driver had consumed drugs, but also that the drugs had rendered him incapable of having proper control of the vehicle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: For instance, where Police officers arrive only after an incident has occurred, a positive blood test alone may not be sufficient.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is because it may not be possible to prove that the drugs had impaired driving, unless there is evidence, such as in-car camera footage showing such impairment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Ministry of Home Affairs has reviewed this and assessed that there should not be a need to prove impaired driving.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Driving with the presence of specified substances in one's blood is itself dangerous and should be deterred, since these specified substances – for example, etomidate – are already regulated under our existing laws and are known to impair driving ability by affecting reaction time, attention and coordination.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Sim Ann, if I may ask you to just take a seat.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Sim Ann, you may proceed to resume your speech.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We recognise that there may be situations where a person lawfully consumes or administers specified substances for medicinal purposes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Bill provides a statutory defence where the substance was lawfully consumed by or administered; and the person did not know or have reason to believe that consuming it could impair his or her driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, if the consumption of such substances did in fact impair the driving of the person, then there would continue to be criminal liability, as per the existing law.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The third objective of this Bill is to enhance Traffic Police's ability to detect and enforce against traffic offences, in four areas.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Currently, enforcement of drink-driving is a two-stage process.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Upon suspicion of drink-driving, an officer administers a preliminary breath test at the roadside.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: If the result is positive, the driver is arrested and brought to the Police lock-up, where an evidential-grade breath test is administered.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This process is operationally onerous and results in a lower alcohol concentration reading when the evidential-grade breath test is carried out at the lock-up.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It is also unnecessary as technology has improved over the years and Handheld Breath Analysers can now provide evidential-grade test results.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police can also conduct its drink driving enforcement operations more efficiently without having to bring the driver to the lock-up.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Second, the Bill aligns the procedure in the RTA for the taking of breath and blood specimens from hospital patients with that of similar provisions in the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Currently, under the RTA, before a police officer may require a hospital patient to provide a blood specimen to determine his blood alcohol level, the registered medical practitioner in immediate charge of the patient must first authorise this.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: While the Act does not prescribe the mode or manner of obtaining the authorisation, in a recent judgement, the District Court held that this authorisation must be express – that is, it cannot be inferred from the doctor's silence or failure to object.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In that case, the drink driving suspect was acquitted after the doctor treating him was found not to have explicitly authorised the taking of a blood specimen.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This differs from the process under the Criminal Procedure Code, which governs forensic medical examinations in non-traffic investigative contexts and does not impose similar express authorisation requirement on the treating medical practitioner.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In its place, before taking a blood specimen, the medical practitioner or nurse in immediate charge of the patient must be satisfied that the taking of the specimen will not endanger the individual.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The amendment removes the procedural authorisation requirement but does not diminish the medical practitioner's or nurse's duty to assess whether doing so would harm the patient.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The safety of the patient remains paramount and continues to be assured with this amendment.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Third, the Bill amends section 65B of the RTA, which sets out the offence of using a mobile communication device while driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Currently, an offender must satisfy three elements to be liable for an offence: (a) the driver must hold the mobile communication device in his hand; (b) the driver must operate any communicative or other functions of the device; and (c) the vehicle must be in motion while the driver is holding and operating the device.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The requirement in element (b) – that the driver must operate a function of the device – can only be enforced by a Police officer on the ground who observes the driver operating the device while the vehicle is in motion.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: More importantly, there should be no need to prove that the driver was operating the device.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Unlike other everyday objects, a mobile communication device is ordinarily held to communicate or access information.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These are activities which typically require the driver's visual and cognitive attention and divert their attention away from driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where the device is handheld, the risk of distraction is further compounded because the driver must hold and support the device, reducing the driver's ability to maintain proper control of the vehicle.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: A driver who holds a mobile communication device in his hand while the vehicle is in motion will commit an offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This amendment also makes clear that it is not an offence if the device is secured in a mount and a driver touches it while driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, where the driver's use of a mounted device distracts the driver or compromises the driver's control of the vehicle, the driver may be liable for offences such as careless or dangerous driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Fourth, the Bill supports the Traffic Police's ongoing efforts to leverage technology to scale up enforcement of traffic violations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Today, when a camera captures a vehicle committing a traffic violation, a Police officer must review the footage to determine whether there is sufficient evidence that an offence has been committed and, if so, require the owner of the vehicle to provide the particulars of the driver at the time of the alleged offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police will ensure that only computer programs that have been robustly tested are used for enforcement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The computer program will also be subject to regular audits to ensure its continued accuracy and reliability.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where such application is made, an officer will manually review the relevant evidence that led to the issuance of the notice.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Bill also makes two other amendments to streamline and clarify existing provisions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The current legal language in the RTA may give rise to an interpretation that a driving disqualification period runs concurrently with an imprisonment term in certain contexts – meaning an offender effectively serves his disqualification while incarcerated and already unable to drive.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In a case earlier this year, an offender was convicted of drink driving and other unrelated offences.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: He was not imprisoned for drink driving, but imprisoned for the unrelated offences.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Court of Appeal interpreted section 67(2) of the RTA to mean that the offender's disqualification period should commence on the date of his drink driving conviction, despite the offender being in prison for unrelated offences.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Last year, there had been a spike in both the numbers and seriousness of traffic accidents and this Bill is timely in raising the seriousness of traffic-related offences as well as making them easier to prosecute.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, there are a range of amendments dealing with penalties for causing death and grievous hurt.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: My question is whether this is necessary as I believe such a person can probably be prosecuted under existing offences where such a person can be charged for intending to cause death or grievous hurt under the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Penal Code covers a whole spectrum of mens rea, from intentional harm to causing it by a rash or negligent act, with different penalties for each.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Jarrett Tee case mentioned by the Minister could, perhaps, have been categorised as intentional causing of grievous hurt since he had asked his passengers if they wanted to see the motorcycle fly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And after the incident, he had said, she deserved it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, it sounds like this was intention to cause grievous hurt and could alternatively have been brought under that offence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this regard, I will be grateful if the Minister can clarify whether there is an envisioned overlap in the current legislation that this needs to fill on the basis that the RTA is not the only legislation that can deal with this situation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If more than one Act might apply in a situation, such as the Penal Code, how would the authorities decide which Act to apply?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are other amendments that raise the penalties for dangerous and careless driving causing grievous hurt, and I agree with the rationale that grievous hurt can totally ruin a person's life and causing it should be treated with a suitably serious penalty.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Second, I note the offence of handphone driving is now going to be easier to make out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The requirement for the driver to actually be using the phone has been removed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I note that there is a new section 65B(1B) which provides that, "to avoid doubt…a driver who touches with his or her hand a mobile communication device which is secured in a mounting affixed to the vehicle, in the manner intended by the manufacturer of the mounting, does not hold the device." So, this gives some clarity to what many drivers have been doing, which is, using mounted mobile devices while they drive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, this clearly is not going to be an offence anymore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think this clarity is helpful, particularly for those in the private hire trade who rely on this for a living.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I also agree with the clarification that should their use of the mobile device surmount to carelessness, then they would face potential liability under careless driving.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While I have no objections to these offences being treated more seriously, I do have some concerns about a purely presence-based model without the need to show either intoxication or a suitably high level of concentration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, intoxicating substances, include glue, paint and petrol fumes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Under the Intoxicating Substances Act, an offence is committed if a person inhales these substances for the purpose of causing or inducing himself to be in a state of intoxication.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, if a person inhales these substances without such an intention, such as in the course of work, say working at a petrol station, construction site or factory, they will not commit an offence under the Intoxicating Substances Act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, for those people who are exposed to intoxicating substances in the course of work, because of workplace safety requirements, they are unlikely to inhale them in sufficient quantities to get intoxicated though there will probably be some level of these substances in their blood because they will be inhaling it.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Some of these people may drive as a living, for example, vehicle operators at construction sites, while others may drive cars or motorcycles to work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Next, on the amendments to do away with a manual review in favour of automated notices, I think this is sensible from the perspective of administrative efficiency and saving resources, and I am grateful for the Minister's clarification that this will only be confined to offences where machines are able to confirm with a high level of certainty that an offence has been committed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If the aim is to keep the person off the road, I think it does not really matter what the reason is.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the outset, I wish to state clearly that I support the main proposals for change to our Road Traffic laws under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The data shared by MHA paints a stark picture between 2021 and 2025.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To arrest this worrying trend, firmer legislative mechanisms are undoubtedly required.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I fully support the introduction of penalties for purposeful endangerment, the tightening of legal alcohol limits, the standalone drug driving framework and the transition towards automated enforcement technology.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, the creation of a purposeful endangerment framework addresses a critical gap where a driver deliberately uses a vehicle as a dangerous weapon.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As the Ministry has noted, such offenders often cannot be convicted of murder or culpable homicide because of the exceptionally high threshold of proving intention to kill or knowledge that death was likely to result.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Instead, they are typically charged with dangerous driving causing death, which currently carries a maximum imprisonment term of eight years for a first-time offender.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my speech today, I seek to clarify the understanding and practical enforcement of certain provisions, with particular focus on the evolving definitions surrounding mobile communication devices, digital screens and mounted devices while driving.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill amends the offence of using a communication device to simply holding one, thereby allowing Traffic Police officers to enforce the offence without needing to prove active device use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I welcome the Government's intention to make our roads safer by reducing distractions caused by motorists handling their mobile devices while driving.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: These distractions no longer arise only from handheld phones.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They increasingly come from mounted smartphones, wearable devices, large infotainment systems, digital dashboards and other screens embedded within modern vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: As vehicles become more technologically advanced, our regulatory frameworks must also continue to keep pace with the changing nature of driver distraction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under this Bill, a driver is not regarded as holding a device if the device is mounted in accordance with the mount manufacturer's intended use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I understand the practical rationale for this exemption, it raises important questions about how the exemption will operate alongside existing road safety rules.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In March 2026, I asked the Minister for Home Affairs whether the Ministry had conducted or reviewed any local studies on the impact of multiple mounted mobile devices or digital screens on motorist reaction times and overall driving performances.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Ministry instead noted that Rule 126 of the Road Traffic (Motor Vehicles, Construction and Use) Rules already makes it an offence to install a visual display unit in the manner that causes distraction or constitutes a safety hazard.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given the absence of local research, I continue to urge the Ministry to proactively study the effects of screen-based distractions on road safety.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In particular, we need empirical evidence on whether multiple mounted devices, large dashboard screens and simultaneous digital interfaces affect driver cognitive load, situation awareness and emergency braking response times.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such data will enable policy makers to calibrate future regulations on a sound evidential basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under the Bill, the touching and operation of a properly mounted device will not amount to the offence of holding a communication device.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, the same device could potentially still constitute a visual distraction under Rule 126 depending on how it is installed and used.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can the Minister clarify how these two provisions are intended to interact?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: What would legally constitute a safe mounting arrangement under the new framework?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Would compliance with the mounting requirements under the Bill have any bearing on the assessment of whether a visual display unit creates a distraction under Rule 126?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We must also consider the realities faced by many platform workers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Each additional screen potentially imposes further cognitive demands on the driver and increases the amount of visual attention diverted from the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Has the Ministry assessed whether the use of multiple mounted devices contributes significantly to driver distraction?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If not, would it consider studying this issue and also to study how safe driving can be enhanced, whether by way of improving vehicle dashboard or device design, hardware or software, particularly given the growing number of drivers who rely on platform work as a source of income, for their safety?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Beyond mobile phones and wearables, the law must also keep pace with developments in vehicle design itself.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Modern infotainment systems have evolved into sophisticated communication and entertainment hubs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Features such as Apple Car Play, Android Auto, allow motorists to send messages, browse media content, interact with navigation systems while their vehicles are in motion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: At the same time, many manufacturers have adopted increasingly minimalist cockpit designs, replacing traditional buttons and switches with large touchscreen interfaces.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Functions that were once operated instinctively through physical controls are increasingly accessed through digital menus, requiring drivers to glance away from the road even for routine tasks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: So, Mr Deputy Speaker, while stronger penalties are necessary, enforcement alone cannot fully address the problem if the design of modern vehicle cockpits is itself becoming a source of distraction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If we focus solely on penalising distracted driving after it occurs without examining whether certain vehicle designs contribute to driver distraction in the first place, we may be addressing the symptoms rather than the cause.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Around the world, regulators and vehicle-safety bodies are increasingly recognising that road safety depends not merely on how people drive, but also how vehicles are designed to be operated.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In Europe, European New Car Assessment Programme has revised the safety assessment protocols to encourage manufacturers to retain physical controls for key vehicle functions in response to concerns about touchscreen-related driver distraction.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Similarly, China has introduced requirement for designated safety-critical vehicle functions to retain dedicated haptic physical controls that can be located and operated by touch alone, reducing the need for drivers to take their eyes off the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the United States (US), the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has also issued driver distraction guidelines, recommending that certain visual manual tasks be restricted or locked up while a vehicle is in motion where they may interfere excessively with driver attention.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Does the Government agree that safety-critical vehicle controls should remain readily operable, without prolonged visual interaction with digital screens or navigation through multiple layers of menus?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, we must send a clear and unequivocal message that irresponsible and dangerous behaviour on our roads will not be tolerated.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: (In Mandarin): Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the measures in the Bill to strengthen road safety, including introducing the offence of purposefully endangering safety, tightening drink-driving standards and expanding the use of automated enforcement technology.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With technological advancement, the distractions faced by drivers are no longer limited to mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many vehicles are equipped with large touchscreens and various digital systems, and drivers can likewise be distracted when operating these devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I support this Bill. : Mr Deputy Speaker, I support this Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The case for action is compelling, traffic fatalities hit a 10-year high is 2025.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The rising numbers of traffic accidents resulting in injuries also increased and the number of traffic violations rose too.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such evidence should be of great concern to drivers who transport people and goods daily, the workers who use our roads for commuting and their families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And the introduction and implementation of stronger laws must be aimed at supporting their safety on our roads.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It targets drivers who deliberately endanger any other road user.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They deliberately use their vehicle to pose a safety risk to another on the road.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill recognises that difference, and calls it "purposeful endangerment", and metes out stiff penalties for introducing dangers to our roads.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This should make our roads much safer for workers like our bus captains, taxi and private hire drivers and delivery workers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our roads are their workplaces and their families just want them to return home safely after work ends.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In July this year, it was reported that the number of work-related traffic fatalities in the first half of 2025 has exceeded last year's total.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I would ask the Ministry to commit to a review in a few years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Did identifying this new offence actually shift driver behaviour?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Higher numbers of violations in the statute book are not proof of success.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Lower fatality and injury numbers on the ground are.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Section 63A(6) empowers a District or Magistrate's Court to impose the full penalty.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This departs from the usual position under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And confirm that rights of appeal remain fully preserved?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Could the Minister share concrete outreach timeline before the commencement?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Would the Minister consider a targeted campaign well ahead of the first summons and delivered through the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), the platform operators and the taxi associations?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I have noted the proactive clarification by the Ministry in its media release, that the usage of mounted devices will not be an offence and that drivers may also hold their devices while the vehicle is stationery.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is an important clarification to ease concerns on the ground.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many platform workers receive their in-app notifications on their phone and rely on them for navigation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I urge the Ministry to leverage on my proposed campaign to ensure that our platform workers are kept up-to-date.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Clauses 11 and 13 create a new offence for any specified substance found in a driver's blood.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But the burden falls on the driver to prove his use was lawful.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I note that doctors and pharmacists do highlight the side effects of prescribed medicines, including when the medications affect a person's fitness to drive and operate machinery.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I therefore ask the Ministry to continue to work with pharmacies to highlight when a prescribed medication could affect the driver's fitness and to provide a simple hotline a driver can call to enquire before he starts his shift, and not after he is being arrested?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, on the disqualification timing, where disqualification begins after release from prison.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I agree with the Ministry that errant and dangerous drivers should be kept away from our roads.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, this poses an adverse impact on breadwinners where driving was part of their job.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I therefore ask that when livelihoods are affected, that the Ministry work with platform operators, our unions and platform work associations, and NTUC's Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) in the outreach and in handling of cases sensitively.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In this regard, I would like to take this opportunity to thank the Ministry for its recent efforts to engage unions and platform work associations leaders before revising the Driver Improvement Points System.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I hope that the Ministry can adopt the same consultative approach to manage the livelihood issues in the transition towards the new compliance measures being debated today.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It allows a computer program to assess camera footage.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: That program can then automatically trigger notices to vehicle owners.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As enforcement becomes more technology-enabled, Singaporeans must remain confident that technology assists decisions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is important that section 81A clarifies that this computer program is operated under the Deputy Commissioner of Police's oversight.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And I would like to ask the Minister four questions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: First, will the human review safeguard remain permanent, to safeguard accountability even as the confidence in the system continues to grow?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Second, will the appeal process remain fast and free-of-charge?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Fourth, how will the Ministry maintain transparency and provide timely information to road users on which offences are being handled by the computer program?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such a driver will feel the pinch of loss of income if they are unable to drive while their case is under appeal.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How will the Ministry handle appeals of those detected by the computer system and resolve them quickly?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, on the record-keeping duties for corporate vehicle owners under section 81C.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay): Sir, for many Malay/Muslim drivers and delivery riders, this job is not merely about earning a living.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The duty to return home to one's family each night in good health.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These are the values that have long guided our community on the roads.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Viewed through this lens, this Bill is aligned with our principles.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It imposes heavy penalties on those who wilfully endanger others.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, allow me to raise two concerns that better reflect the reality of our community.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: For private-hire vehicle drivers, taxi drivers and food delivery riders, the phone is not merely a communication device.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a work device to determine the next job, the delivery address and the day's earnings.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The new regulations must be explained in detail.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This clarity is important so that a driver does not lose his licence due to confusion, not negligence.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many elderly drivers in our community have diabetes, high blood pressure or heart conditions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They take medication every day in order to continue working and supporting their families.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This Bill introduces new offences relating to certain substances in a driver's blood.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While legal defences exist, the burden falls on the driver himself.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Because to a father who supports his family with this income, losing his licence means losing his livelihood.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And the loss of his livelihood affects the entire family, including his school-going children.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This "amanah" or duty is not only meant for the road.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It also applies at home. : Mr Deputy Speaker, this Bill does right on three fronts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Our commuters deserve safer roads and so, they can arrive at home safely to their families.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is more than 150% higher than in Tokyo and almost double Hong Kong's.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Road-related deaths are a leading non-health related cause of death in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Perhaps, it will also help to start avoiding using the word "accidents", which may in a way imply inevitability and helplessness, weaken accountability and also reduce needed attention to root causes, which ultimately can be tackled through public policy and infrastructure design.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Broadly speaking, the tools added or amended before this House operate to tackle road traffic incidents via four mechanisms: first, boosting certainty, that is, the chance of getting caught; two, severity of consequences; three, removing the ability to offend; four, norm signalling.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Each of these areas have room for improvement or greater clarity, both in the legislation and in the public policy being effected on the ground.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Clause 10 changes section 65B from an offence requiring both the holding and operation of a mobile communication device to an offence based on holding the device while the vehicle is in motion.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This should make the offence more straightforward to enforce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, the clause also makes clear that merely touching a phone secured in a properly affixed holder does not amount to holding it.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Repeating the call by my colleague, Mr Dennis Tan, could the Minister clarify how the law will address drivers who interacts extensively with a mounted phone or even entertainment system?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This could include typing messages, scrolling through social media, watching videos or taking video calls.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What rules will apply, where the same activities are carried out through an in-vehicle display, including through systems, such as Apple CarPlay.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: At what point will such conduct be enforced as careless or dangerous driving under sections 65 or 64?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The other point on enforcement relates to enforcement cameras.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Bill touches on cameras, my question relates to a broader point.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Enforcement camera locations these days are publicly disclosed and flagged out in bright colours, as it was noted that this is important for deterrence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet in 2024, the Traffic Police released statistics that showed that motorists would slow down to ensure they are not caught and then go back to speeding again after they have cleared the stretch.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that vehicle velocity is the most important determinant of crash deaths, I am concerned that this behaviour not only fails to reduce speeding or dangerous driving.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It may instead cause drivers to drive more dangerously when they believe there is no chance of being caught.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, what is the evidence that the current format of disclosed camera and ad hoc Traffic Police enforcement is sufficient to tackle excessive speeds and dangerous driving?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Clause 7 raises the imprisonment ceilings for reckless or dangerous driving causing grievous hurt under section 64, including for repeat and serious repeat offenders.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Clause 8, likewise, raises certain additional imprisonment ceilings for serious offenders convicted of careless driving causing grievous hurt while leaving the existing fines unchanged.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could the Minister explain what evidence and methodology used to assess whether the Act's statutory dollar denominated fine limits remain sufficiently deterrent for motorists of very different means?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Does MHA examine its sentencing outcomes, repeat offending and the relative burden of fines across offenders' financial circumstances?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While penalties, like jail terms and suspensions, ultimately remove the ability to re-offend, a crime punishment model alone is not enough.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to bring down offending in the first place by rethinking our road infrastructure.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some positive steps have been taken recently with initiatives to calm traffic, improve pedestrian use and access.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is worth reiterating that alongside intelligent design with direct input from behavioural signs, traffic calming results in lower speed limits, and lower speed limits result in lower casualties.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Recent Meta analysis studies from different cities show that a 30 km/h speed limit in urban areas causes an average 40% reduction in crashes, fatalities and injuries, with added benefits in improving active mobility and health.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A 30 km/h speed limit may also not need to mean longer travel times if we design our roads to improve traffic flow by reducing stopping times, allowing closer spacing and making lane merging easier.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, while we already have the Green Link Determining system determining our traffic light junctions' timings, could we not upgrade this further to improve safety?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In order to do so, we also need to pay attention to the end-user experience; that is, to ensure that traffic light timings do not end up making motorists even more impatient and likely to speed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can the Minister clarify if or how our traffic lights control system takes similar measures into account?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Other traffic calming measures, especially for new roads, should also be rolled out quicker and there should be better centralisation of efforts with input from road users and experts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would also provide more learning points from where existing roads and Silver Zones can and should be improved.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During our Sengkang Town Hall conversations a couple of years back, residents also shared their candid views and thoughts about already worsening road safety standards and increased congestion.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What became clear to many of us then was the sense that relief and deterrence measures were important, but only a part of the puzzle.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We wanted to know why motorists were acting the way they did; that is, to get to the root cause of the problem.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Why are we speeding more and driving more recklessly?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What is the impact on road safety of increased stress, population density and crowding on the way we drive, react and act on our roads?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What does the data show and how do we tackle these root causes of poor road safety beyond throwing more people in jail or impounding vehicles and revoking licences?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The reduced alcohol limits introduced by clause 19 signal new norms in another way to change the culture of driving in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My WP colleague, Mr Andre Low, will speak more on this but hopefully, this is a start to shift the needle away from the attitude that a motorist can drink as long as they can handle their alcohol.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This takes a leaf from global aviation industry efforts to eliminate fatalities from incidents and akin to what we are aiming for, for workplace health and safety.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Sweden, Norway and Finland work on efforts across policy-makers, enforcement agencies and all sectors of society to find and implement ways to virtually eliminate all traffic fatalities, buttressed by the ultimate belief that loss of life on roads is both preventable and unacceptable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is not an easy task, especially as individual failings account for many deaths, but we must work continuously to ensure that our roads and their design keep up with innovation and technology for vehicles, and to more holistically regulate and encourage road safety.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is time for us to set our own North Star in our own attempt to do so.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As an orthopaedic surgeon, I have had to treat many victims of road traffic accidents.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The public often remembers the headlines, the collisions, the fatalities, the Court cases.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But in hospitals and in the emergency rooms, we remember something very different.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We remember the young motorcyclist who survives but spends months in rehabilitation, recovering from multiple fractures and repeated surgeries.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We remember the pedestrian who never walks independently again.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We remember the father who can no longer work because of chronic pain; the mother who has to become both a caregiver and a breadwinner; and the child whose life quietly changes because someone else's momentary lapse became a lifelong consequence.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These are the stories that seldom make the news, but they are the very reasons that this House is debating this Bill today.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is also about preventing lifelong disability, protecting livelihoods and keeping families together.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The objective of this Bill is therefore not simply to punish more drivers.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For me, this Bill rests on a very simple but important principle: that road safety succeeds when our laws are fair, firm and practical.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Today, I would like to make three points: first, protecting lives; second, protecting livelihoods; and third, protecting public trust.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It recognises that there is a clear distinction between negligence and intent.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Most road accidents arise from human error, but this amendment addresses something different – intentional harm.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Where a vehicle is deliberately used to endanger another person's life, society is dealing with something fundamentally different.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A motor vehicle is no longer simply a mode of transport.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And the law should recognise that distinction, and I am pleased that this Bill does so too.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Simply holding a phone while driving will now constitute an offence while making clear that touching a phone that is mounted does not do so.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Drivers should not be holding a mobile phone while their vehicle is in motion.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our eyes belong on the road and our hands belong on the wheel.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because every distracted glance lasts only a few seconds, but as mentioned earlier, the consequences for some can be a lifetime.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The safest accident is the one that does not happen at all.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Every dangerous driver deterred before causing harm means one fewer patient in our emergency departments.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If there is a genuine risk to public safety, early intervention is the right thing to do.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: However, I would like to seek some clarification from the Minister on how these powers will be exercised in practice.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For many Singaporeans, a driving licence is not simply a licence.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Many of them spend 10 to 12 hours on the road daily.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Their licence essentially pays the mortgage, puts food on the table and pays their children's school fees.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Could the Minister therefore elaborate on the safeguards that will ensure that these suspension powers remain proportionate, transparent and timely?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Could the Minister also assure our professional drivers that appeals involving the livelihoods will be dealt expeditiously?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Where investigations ultimately exonerate a driver, what are the mechanisms that exist to minimise unnecessary disruption to their livelihoods?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We need both because road safety succeeds only when our laws are not only firm, but also when they are fair.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: People accept tough laws and they accept them when they can understand them better.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: If we want safer roads tomorrow, we must educate our road users today better.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Penalties change behaviour through fear but education changes behaviour through intentional choice.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Could the Minister explain how the changes to the law today and the principles behind these changes be weaved into public educational and communication, including across our schools?

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Technology allows us to intervene earlier, apply the law more consistently and improves objectivity.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But I hope we will go one step further.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Technology should become a partnership in prevention, not just merely a tool for punishment.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Perhaps, currently installed cameras and prospectively installed cameras can pick up near misses and such near misses be shared with these drivers to show them what could have been a fatality or something consequential.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Because ultimately, no camera, no sensor, no piece of legislation can replace personal responsibility.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That the people around them will exercise basic care.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The motorcyclist riding home after work, the parent driving a child to school and the pedestrian at a crossing all rely on it.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When someone drives after drinking or taking intoxicating drugs that trust is broken.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The risk is borne not only by the driver but by everyone around them.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A serious injury can change what a person is able to do, how a family lives and what their future looks like forever.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that is why there is often a palpable sense of public anger when someone who did nothing wrong is killed or permanently injured in an avoidable collision.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our task as Parliamentarians is not to amplify that anger but to tap into it, so that it can inform our work to reduce the chances of the next tragedy.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The law cannot undo irreversible harm, but it can set clearer boundaries, support effective enforcement and make dangerous choices far less likely.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My comments today will focus on the changes concerning drink and drug driving and the evidence on which these offences will be enforced.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The legal limit should not be mistaken for permissive drinking allowance.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a substantial change intended to shift behaviour as much as enforcement.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I ask the Minister to explain the evidence supporting the precise limits of 15 microgrammes and 30 milligrammes that we have chosen, including the relationship between these levels and the risk of impaired driving.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also asked how the new limits will be communicated to the public.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MHA's safest advice in their press release is that drivers should not drink at all.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Public messaging should reinforce that norm rather than invite motorists to guess at how much they might be able to consume without crossing the line.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That message must be matched by an enforcement people can trust.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill will also allow evidential breath test to be conducted at or near the place where the requirement is made.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MHA intends to use portable handheld breath evidential analysers at the scene.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Faster testing may give a reading closer to the time of the offence, but that roadside reading may also become central evidence in a criminal case.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The more consequential the reading, the more important is that the device can withstand scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What approval, calibration and maintenance standards will apply and how will measurement uncertainty rounding and device tolerances be treated where a reading is at or very near the legal limit?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And where these records are relevant to the prosecution, would the accused be able to obtain the device calibration and operator records needed to test the evidence?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The need for a clear and defensible legal boundary is even more important for drug driving.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under the present framework, enforcement may require proof that a driver was unfit and incapable of proper control.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Different substances can affect people differently and proving the precise link between a substance and a driver's impairment may be difficult.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A presence-based offence gives the law a clearer enforcement line.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MHA should publish the relevant detection windows, its treatment of therapeutic use and any reporting or prosecution thresholds before the offence commences.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Motorists must know the legal boundary and the Courts must be able to assess the evidence consistently.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill already provides a defence for lawful use, including prescribed medication.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The defendant must prove on the balance of probabilities that a substance was lawfully consumed or administered, and that he or she did not know or have reason to believe it would affect proper control of the vehicle.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Its practical operation is also very much important.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In practice, I ask what evidence will ordinarily establish lawful use?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it a prescription, a dispensing record or medical evidence?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: MHA should also explain how the test of reason to believe will apply, where medicine carries only a general warning that it may cause drowsiness and what guidance patients, doctors and pharmacists will receive before commencement of this Act.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Once credible medical evidence is produced, the Minister should explain why the defendant should continue to bear the legal burden of proving both parts of the defence.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should be firm against drug driving without leaving responsible patients to interpret a criminal law boundary from a generic label on the medicine packet.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The same principle should also govern how evidence is collected in hospital.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Bill changes the procedure for taking breath and blood specimens from hospital patients and expands the role of nurses.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will the Minister confirm that the patient treatment remains paramount and that a specimen will not be taken where the clinician responsible for the patient's care believes it would compromise their care or treatment?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am glad we are taking these steps and I support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I rise in support of the Road Traffic (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At one level, this Bill is about stronger penalties for dangerous driving.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But at a deeper level, it is about something more fundamental: trust.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Every day, millions of Singaporeans place their trust in people they have never met.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We trust that the driver approaching a pedestrian crossing will slow down.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We trust that the motorist beside us is paying attention.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We trust that the person behind the wheel has chosen not to drink, not to speed recklessly and not to look at a mobile phone while driving.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Dangerous driving is a breach of that shared trust and that is why I support this Bill.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The purpose of stronger penalties is not punishment for its own sake.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is to influence behaviour before harm occurs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Every driver who chooses to slow down because the consequences are more severe represents an accident that does not happened.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Every motorist who chooses to keep both eyes on the road because enforcement is more credible represents a family spared unimaginable grief.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some may ask whether stronger penalties alone are enough.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But that does not make them any less necessary.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The statistics show why this Bill is timely.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And Singaporeans have been shocked by high profile cases like the June 2024 Central Expressway racing case.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Each statistic represents a life altered, a family grieving, or a future forever changed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I fully support the Bill's central changes, including the new offence of purposeful endangerment and the increased penalties for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Where a driver knowingly or deliberately puts another person's life at risk, the law should reflect the full seriousness of that choice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: These provisions are proportionate to the harm they address.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I do want to raise one question on the Bill's mobile phone provision, and a separate concern about how, in the context of these tougher penalties, the recently announced revised demerit points regime will affect our private hire and taxi drivers.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, prosecutors must prove a driver was actively using a handheld device.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill removes that requirement – simply holding a phone while the vehicle is moving will be enough, enforceable by camera or by footage support submitted by members of the public.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I understand the underlying logic: distraction begins before a call connects or a message is typed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But removing the need to prove active use also removes the safeguard that previously separated genuinely risky conduct from momentary, non-distracting contact – a driver silencing a ringing phone, repositioning it on a mount, passing it to a passenger or rerouting using a maps apps after making a wrong turn or running into traffic.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister clarify what threshold Traffic Police and the Courts will apply in practice to distinguish these situations, and what checks will be in place around footage submitted by members of the public, given that this offence may now be established without any need to show that the driver was distracted at all?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, I want to speak up for our private hire and taxi drivers on the demerit points changes in the context of higher penalties.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The intent: to get irresponsible motorists off the road sooner.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For most motorists, an occasional suspension is a serious inconvenience.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For a private hire or taxi driver, it is their livelihood.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I acknowledge that the Ministry has introduced a one-time point adjustment to ease the transition in direct response to concerns raised by vocational drivers and transport unions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This shows that the Ministry is alive to the issue.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It does not address the ongoing, structurally higher exposure that vocational drivers face every year, simply by virtue of spending far more hours on the road than the average motorist and depending on that same licence for their income.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They would likely also be more susceptible to the new mobile phone rules as they use their mobile phones to confirm rides and receive messages from platform operators.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I ask the Minister whether there is a case for more support measures specific to this group, such as reconsidering some variant of the Safe Driving Course in lieu of a portion of suspension time?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I raise this not to weaken the deterrent effect of the new regime but because if we are asking one group of road users to bear a disproportionate livelihood risk in service of a safety goal that we all share, this House should at least examine whether targeted support is warranted, in the same way we have looked at safeguards in other sectors undergoing regulatory tightening.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Singapore's good road safety record has never depended on a single intervention.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Good laws, consistent enforcement, safer road design, public education and responsible road users all reinforce each other.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill strengthens one pillar: personal responsibility backed by credible deterrence.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: First, technology can make enforcement smarter, not just stricter.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Deterrence depends on certainty of detection, not only severity of punishment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The rise in red-light running accidents suggests detection at certain locations remains a live gap.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister share how the Traffic Police and LTA are using, or plan to use anonymised traffic data and artificial intelligence- (AI-) assisted analysis to spot emerging hotspots before they produce repeated accidents, and to deploy enforcement dynamically to where the risk is highest?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It should make enforcement more targeted and more preventive.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, every serious accident should sharpen our understanding, not just our accountability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Each is a tragedy, but also a chance to learn why it happened and whether patterns point to fixes in design, enforcement or education.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on how these lessons are systematically fed back into policy and whether better data capabilities can help us move from responding to accidents towards anticipating them?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Deterrence and learning are about correcting for the minority who put others at risk.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we should not lose sight of the majority who already drive responsibly, day after day.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I was glad to see the Traffic Police's own "Reward the Sensible Motorists" initiative, recognising exemplary drivers for safe behaviour.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I would ask the Ministry to consider scaling this up and pairing it with the driving data that fleet operators and insurers increasingly hold, so that safe behaviour is recognised systematically, not only symbolically.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Spain's points-based licensing system offers a model worth studying here.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A Bill about deterrence should sit alongside a system that also rewards doing the right things.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have more active seniors, more cyclists, more users of active mobility devices, more delivery riders.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This diversity makes mutual respect on our roads more important than ever.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to be more careful, more patient.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Road safety is not about prioritising one group of users over another, it is about ensuring that everyone on four wheels, two wheels or on foot can reach their destination safely.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If it works, those numbers should eventually fall.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With the privilege of using our roads comes the responsibility to use them safely.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill is not about punishing more drivers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, I would like to clarify the intent of section 63(a), "purposeful endangerment using motor vehicle".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In March, I asked the Ministry whether we needed an offence of vehicular homicide with penalties on par with culpable homicide due to the mens rea hurdle rates of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The reply was that such an offence was being considered and described it in almost the exact terms now before us as section 63(a).

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I welcome it, and that is why I would like to understand its boundaries.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Its middle limb requires the purpose to endanger "a particular person".

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In March, the Ministry said it would be "another person" and the Bill's three illustrations are all of one driver against another.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, does section 63(a) apply to these two examples: (a) a driver who drives at a crowd meaning to hurt whoever is in front of his or her car, taking out nobody in particular; (b) a driver who drives at a tree with the intent to kill him or herself.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, why did the Government choose to retain this eight-year ceiling for causing death?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Third, we will need firmer measures against drivers who are on the road when they should not be there at all.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
