text: The driver who is caught is banned and the driver who has lost his or her licence and never earned it back.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like the Government to consider a minimum sentence for this offence.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Government has said that they would work with the Sentencing Advisory Panel on guidelines for drink-driving.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, forfeiture of the vehicle is mandatory only on a second conviction for driving while disqualified.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Would it consider making it mandatory for the first?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three, our annual Road Traffic Report tells us how many speedsters and drunk drivers we catch, but not how many disqualified or unlicensed drivers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will the Government publish that number and how many of them go on to re-offend?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I would just like to also put forward my approval and agreement with the Member Mariam Jaafar's earned buffer system.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I have had residents with 10-year clean records with a single high demerit point offence, which have endangered their private hire vehicle driving livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some consideration of their long-term clean history should be given, so as to better take the circumstances into account.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications and suggestions, I support the Bill and its aim of making our roads safer.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And I therefore will not quote any numbers, but I will definitely support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I have three points for the Minister to consider.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I have personally encountered people brake check in front of me, so it falls under the purposeful endangerment clause.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I watched a couple of videos online also and it is really, really scary.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: My second point is on the issue of riders.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We differentiate between motorists and riders, and in this specific case I am referring to cyclists.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I do notice that there are a lot of cyclists nowadays on the road and some of them may not be familiar with our highway code.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Else, it is quite endangering because they might do things that are not in line with our process, especially if they are from overseas.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The third point is on the automated decision-making process.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I really support this, because I personally, and my wife also, we have encountered, when we receive our speed summonses, quite some time after the offence or the speeding has been done.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I actually support the speeding cameras being deployed.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The issue is not that we want to speed.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: The issue is that there are some speed cameras, but sometimes they are very difficult to see or observe, or it is new.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, I think the point is the shaping of behaviour and therefore, the request is to make sure that if there are any speeding cameras, newly installed speeding cameras, that these be prominently displayed and notified to the motorists.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I can understand that using the automated enforcement or decision-making process, we can quickly get it out, get the details out, especially on the car numbers and asking for the details of the drivers that have committed the offence.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: When the information has been decided and disseminated to the driver that is under the offence, typically we go by mail and that takes about a couple of days.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In this instance where there are new speed cameras, people may use the same road a couple of times per day or within the week.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: And within that week, or before we receive the notice of the offence, we may have committed the offence a couple of times already.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, maybe one solution is that we do an immediate electronic notice.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, that is the grace period for the Minister to consider.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin): I support the Road Traffic (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: First, regarding the act of malicious or deliberate emergency braking, stronger measures should be taken to clamp down on such behaviour.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Bicycles are increasingly common on major roads, making road traffic and driving conditions more complex.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I would therefore like the Minister to consider whether regulations can be introduced to require all cyclists on public roads to pass an examination on road traffic rules or the Highway Code.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: My final point concerns the running of red lights.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I support the use of automated decision-making systems to determine whether running a red light constitutes a traffic violation.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: What I would like to know is whether, when a new red light or speeding enforcement system is installed at a location, more prominent signage can be put up to alert drivers that speed enforcement is in effect at that location.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, when a new speed enforcement site is first set up, some drivers may be unaware that enforcement has commenced there.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: In such cases, could a grace period of a few days be granted after traffic infringement notices are issued to him? : Mr Deputy Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, the rapid expansion of the platform economy has brought about many more delivery riders on our roads, many of whom rely on Power-Assisted Bicycles (PABs).

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, our active mobility framework has rightly prioritised pedestrian safety by requiring PABs to use the carriageway instead of footpaths.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a result, our roads now accommodate a broader mix of users travelling at different speeds, operating different types of vehicles and using the roads in very different ways.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This complexity will only increase as autonomous vehicles become part of Singapore's transport network.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As interactions between road users become more complex, the margin for error narrows.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A single moment of distraction or poor judgement can have far more serious consequences, particularly for vulnerable road users.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our enforcement regime and deterrence framework must therefore evolve alongside these challenges.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Against this backdrop, I support the broad intent of the Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Strengthening deterrence is therefore both timely and necessary.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But lasting improvements in road safety cannot be achieved through harsher penalties alone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Effective deterrence rests on four pillars: a high certainty of detection, proportionate enforcement, timely behavioural intervention and ultimately, a shared sense of responsibility among all who use our roads.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I support the Bill's move towards stronger penalties for irresponsible road behaviour.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, deterrence depends not only on the severity of punishment, but also on the certainty of detection.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore has never shied away from imposing strong penalties where public safety is at stake.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But penalties alone cannot deter offences that are inherently difficult to detect.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On our roads, many types of dangerous behaviour can last only a few seconds.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A driver may glance at a mobile phone, drift briefly into another lane or make an unsafe manoeuvre before correcting it moments later.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such offences are fleeting by nature and difficult to detect consistently through patrols alone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unless offenders believe that they are likely to be caught, even the harshest of penalties will have limited deterrent effect.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The prohibition against using a mobile phone, as we have heard previously from many speeches, while driving is not new.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Parliament first introduced these restrictions more than two decades ago, when mobile phones were primarily used for voice calls and Short Message Service (SMS).

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, the nature of distraction has fundamentally changed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are cameras, entertainment platforms, navigation systems, social media platforms and even productivity tools.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, beyond making calls or replying to messages, motorists can now watch videos, browse social media or participate in online meetings even while travelling at speed.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is continuous, immersive and far more dangerous.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the risk has evolved, then our enforcement methods must evolve as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Several jurisdictions have begun leveraging technology to strengthen this deterrence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The state of New South Wales in Australia, for example, has deployed AI-powered roadside cameras to detect motorists using hand-held mobile phones while driving.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Rather, AI identifies only potential offences, which are then reviewed and verified by authorised officers before any enforcement action is taken.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This combines the scale and consistency of technology with human judgement and accountability.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond mobile phone offences, are there plans to explore whether similar technologies could detect other unsafe behaviour, such as the failure to wear seat belts, for example?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As enforcement becomes increasingly technology-enabled, robust safeguards will be equally important.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the accuracy of automated detection systems be validated before enforcement action is taken?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What avenues of review will be available to motorists who believe an offence has been wrongly detected?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Public confidence in these technologies will depend not only on their effectiveness but also on their transparency, accuracy and accountability.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Technology should not replace Traffic Police officers; it should amplify their effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By increasing the certainty of detection, it can often deter unsafe behaviour more effectively than increasing penalties alone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The ultimate objective of deterrence is not simply to punish unsafe behaviour, but to change it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For motorists who repeatedly commit distracted driving offences, enforcement should be complemented by targeted behavioural interventions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is particularly relevant for mobile phone use while driving.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Unlike offences arising from excessive speed or inconsiderate driving, distracted driving is often a habitual behaviour.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many motorists do not consciously decide to break the law.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead, they instinctively glance at a notification, attempt to reply to a message, or check a navigation app without fully appreciating the risks.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The programme could focus on behavioural education, hazard perception and the real-life consequences of distracted driving, helping offenders understand that not just that the behaviour is illegal, but also why it is dangerous.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is also scope to strengthen prevention at the earliest stage of a driver's journey.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Driving schools already devote significant attention to vehicle control and traffic rules.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every motorist should demonstrate an understanding of the dangers of distracted driving before obtaining a licence and again, if unsafe habits continue to emerge.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Safer roads are built not only through enforcement, but by changing behaviour.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By combining effective deterrence with meaningful education, we can reduce repeat offending and foster a stronger culture of responsible driving.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I understand why the Government has recently decided on a reduction in the demerit points threshold for licence suspension and the tougher consequences for repeat offenders.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, stronger deterrence is appropriate for those who repeatedly disregard the rules of the road.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By the very nature of their work, they spend substantially more time on our roads than the average motorist and are therefore more likely to accumulate demerit points through sheer exposure alone.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More importantly, their driving licence is not just the privilege; it is also tied to their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I therefore ask whether the Government would consider introducing an early intervention mechanism for vocational drivers.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While, Sir, this should not be viewed as either a relaxation of enforcement or a special concession, attendance for this programme would be compulsory and the intervention would occur well before the suspension threshold is reached and the concession is tightly controlled.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But more importantly, it creates an opportunity to correct unsafe behaviour before a vocational driver loses his or her licence and their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If the objective of the demerit points system is to improve road safety, then timely behavioural intervention is often more effective than waiting until suspension becomes inevitable.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Ultimately, however, no legislation, however comprehensive, can by itself make our roads safer.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not just the responsibility of those who drive, nor is it solely the responsibility of the Traffic Police.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether we drive, ride, cycle, or simply cross the road as pedestrians, every decision we make affects the safety of others.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Respect for the rules, consideration for fellow road users and a willingness to exercise patience and responsibility remain the strongest safeguards against accidents and fatalities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At its heart, road safety has never been about penalties or demerit points.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every accident prevented is potentially a family spared grief.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And every journey completed safely reminds us that the choices we make on our roads matter.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That, Sir, is ultimately, what this Bill seeks to achieve.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I end my speech in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Yet, I wish this Bill had gone even further and made our road traffic laws even stricter – in two ways.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: First, I wish this Bill had also revised the maximum penalty for dangerous driving causing death.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This brings the new offence on par with culpable homicide not amounting to murder under section 304(b) of the Penal Code, even though it could be argued that the offender's state of mind in purposeful endangerment is likely not as egregious and thus, his culpability not as high as in culpable homicide.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Purposefully endangering a person's safety is not quite as egregious as knowing that one's actions are likely to cause death.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: You could purposefully endanger someone without knowing that you are likely to cause death.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Yet the maximum penalty for this new offence of purposeful endangerment on our roads is on par with culpable homicide.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I support the stricter stance, because it will help to keep our roads safe, and keeping our roads safe for all road users is an urgent task and of paramount importance.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, this new offence of purposeful endangerment on our roads causing death carries a maximum penalty of 15 years' jail.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Even though most offenders who cause death while driving will, I think, continue to be prosecuted under the charge of dangerous driving instead of purposeful endangerment, because it will not be that common, I think, for offenders to have the requisite state of mind for a charge of purposeful endangerment to be brought against them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Take the horrific case of Jeremiah Ng, who in 2021 treated our roads like an F1 race track, drove at up to 169 km/h on a 60 km/h road – so, more than 100 km/h an hour above the speed limit – lost control when turning at a T-junction and went straight instead, ploughing into multiple cars on the other side of the T-junction, getting a motorcyclist crushed in between two cars and ultimately, causing one death and leaving six others injured.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Reckless as Jeremiah Ng was, I do not think his state of mind would have met the threshold for purposeful endangerment if this law had existed then.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, he would still have been prosecuted under dangerous driving causing death, with a maximum penalty of eight rather than 15 years' jail.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And that just does not compute for me.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Of course, Jeremiah Ng was also prosecuted as a serious offender because he was also drink driving while driving dangerously, so, there was an additional penalty of up to two more years' jail.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But had he not been drink driving, the maximum penalty would have been eight years.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And for such an egregious case of recklessness and wanton disregard for other road users, eight years' jail feels way too light.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The High Court noted that the "heaviest punishment" for a case like Jeremiah Ng will be the lifelong burden of knowing that his irresponsible and selfish action of dangerous driving while drink driving claimed an innocent life.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But while offenders like him may have a lifetime of guilt and remorse, we cannot count on that.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Our laws should provide for stronger retributive justice.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And so, I wish this Bill had revised the maximum penalty for dangerous driving causing death.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Second, I wish this Bill had also harmonised the offence of dangerous driving causing grievous hurt with the offence of dangerous driving causing death – harmonise the two into one offence of dangerous driving causing death or grievous hurt.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The new offence of purposeful endangerment already includes both death and grievous hurt in one harmonised offence.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And the rationale is simple, that whether or not the victim dies, is not within the control of the offender.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: But his culpability and harm are no less whether the victim dies or not.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: So, one harmonised offence, to deal with his culpability and harm.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: And I think it should be extended to dangerous driving causing death or grievous hurt.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The culpability and harm from causing grievous hurt by dangerous driving may be not be less than causing death.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: This Bill proposes a higher maximum imprisonment penalty for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt, but it is still lower than the maximum penalty for dangerous driving causing death.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: I wish the Bill had brought the offence of dangerous driving causing grievous hurt on par with the offence of dangerous driving causing death, or indeed, harmonise the two.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: Take the case of Yoong Kok Kai, who was heavily drunk, somehow found his way to Tuas Checkpoint, even though he was intending to head north back home.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: He ran down a safety bollard and gantry at Tuas Checkpoint, and drove into an Auxiliary Police Officer who had tried to take refuge behind the safety bollard and gantry from Yoong's car.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong Central)
text: The officer survived the horrific accident, but his injuries have left him permanently incapacitated, unable to eat, unable to move, bathe, dress or toilet without help.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They represent parents, children, friends and colleagues who never make it home.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Behind every number is a family whose lives changed forever.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A resident once shared something with me that has stayed in my mind.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: He runs a small logistics company and often reminds his drivers, "The delivery can be late, but you must go home on time." Mr Speaker, this is exactly what this Bill is about.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But everyone who uses our roads should be able to return home safely.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They spend more time on our roads than most Singaporeans and these amendments will have a direct impact on them.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, I support the new offence of holding a mobile phone while driving.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The current law requires authorities to prove that a driver was actively using the phone.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hands on the wheel, phone on the mount.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is easier for motorists to understand and easier for Traffic Police to enforce.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Importantly, mounted devices remain allowed and drivers may still use their phones when the vehicle is stationary.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This strikes the right balance between road safety and the operational needs of delivery drivers and private hire drivers who depend on navigation for work.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some victims survive but suffer lifelong consequences, like brain injuries, paralysis or permanent disability.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The law should reflect the seriousness of that harm.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The increased penalties send a strong message that irresponsible behaviour on our roads carries serious consequences.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, I support lowering the legal alcohol limit.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Today, the slogan reads: If you drink, do not drive.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But I think it should be reversed: If you drive, do not drink.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: People respond differently to alcohol depending on their body, health and even whether they have eaten.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Trying to calculate "how much is still safe" is not a good habit to encourage.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The new limits also bring Singapore more in line with other advanced jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, introduce a short education-first transition period before full enforcement of the new mobile phone offence.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many delivery riders and drivers have developed habits over many years of checking navigation or delivery applications while driving.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I hope the Traffic Police can consider an advisory period of several months, where first-time offenders receive warnings and educational materials instead of immediate penalties, except in more serious cases.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: During this period, Government agencies can work with platform companies, transport associations and SMEs to publicise the new rules in multiple languages.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The objective is not simply to issue fines; it is to change behaviour.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, help SMEs make every commercial vehicle mount-ready.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many SME operators told me that this is not as straightforward as it sounds.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: One delivery van may be shared by three or four drivers across different shifts.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Instead of every business trying to solve the problem individually, perhaps Government could consider working with LTA and industry to develop a universal phone mount suitable for commercial vehicles.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Support could also be provided to help SMEs retrofit their existing fleets.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In time, such mounts could become standard equipment in newly registered goods vehicles, much like today's in-vehicle units.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When every vehicle already has a suitable mount, safe behaviour becomes the easiest behaviour.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, partner our F&B sector to educate the public on the new alcohol limits.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Many Singaporeans will not know that the legal limit has changed.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Rather than expecting customers to interpret technical guidance about standard drinks or alcohol concentration, the message should remain simple as shared earlier: "If you drive, do not drink." Restaurants, coffee shops and bars can help reinforce this through simple posters, table cards or coasters encouraging customers to take a taxi, use public transport or appoint a designated driver.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Road safety is not solely the responsibility of enforcement agencies; businesses can also play an important role.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill rightly prohibits holding a mobile phone while driving.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, what happens if a phone is properly mounted but is playing videos while the vehicle is moving?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The driver's hands remain on the wheel, but the driver's attention is no longer fully on the road.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, such conduct may only be dealt with under careless or dangerous driving, which still requires proof that the distraction affected the driver's driving.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Does the Ministry intend to monitor this issue?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Would it consider addressing this potential gap in future so that we do not simply shift the distraction from the driver's hand to the phone mount?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Road safety depends not only on good laws but also on responsible choices.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill strengthens both law and our enforcement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With thoughtful implementation and strong public education, it will also help change behaviour before accidents happen.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The delivery can wait, the phone call can wait; but every Singaporean should be able to return home safely.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin): Lastly, road safety ultimately protects each family.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Whenever we leave home, we all hope that we and our loved ones will return home safely.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Obeying traffic rules is not merely a matter of complying with the law; it is also about protecting the loved ones waiting for us at home. : I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: It is a necessary Bill and a timely one.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But there is one gap I hope the Ministry will review and one refinement I hope it will consider.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This Bill is its response and on the whole, it responds well.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Injuries, like brain damage, can leave a victim bedridden for life; the punishment should reflect that.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Careless driving causing serious injury is rightly left unchanged, at two years for a first offence and four for a repeat one.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The larger increase belongs where the conduct is more dangerous, and the Bill gets that balance right.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I welcome, too, the stricter drink driving limits, breath alcohol falling from 35 to 15 microgrammes, blood-alcohol from 80 to 30 milligrammes, bringing us closer to Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The new offence for driving with any trace of a controlled drug or intoxicating substance, even absent visible impairment, closes a real gap.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: And the Bill fixes an old anomaly: a driving ban that used to run down while the offender sat in prison.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The Traffic Police processes hundreds of thousands of violations a year, and today an officer must manually review every photo or video before a Notice to Furnish Driver's Particulars can be issued.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This Bill changes that: for objectively verifiable technical violations, speeding and red-light offences chief among them, the Traffic Police may use an automated decision-making system to assess the violation and issue the Notice without a human reviewing the footage first.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I do not object to this in principle.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: But once a Notice reaches a vehicle owner, the obligation on them is serious – 14 days to identify and furnish the driver's particulars or face prosecution themselves.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Their only recourse against a mistaken Notice is to apply for revocation, reviewed manually, after the fact.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: What the Bill does not do is place any corresponding limit on the Traffic Police's side: how long after an offence is detected the Notice itself may be issued.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: There is a hard 14-day clock running against the owner.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: There is no clock at all running against the system that generates the Notice.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: This imbalance matters more, not less, precisely because the new system is automated and built for the volume MHA has described.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: A system built to run at that scale is also one where a processing backlog can build quietly and go unnoticed until it clears, and by the time a Notice for a months-long violation reaches an owner, the means of checking the system's work may already be gone: dashcam footage overwritten on its usual cycle, a fleet's shift roster long since filed away, memories of who was driving that day faded.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: If a system is fast enough to detect a violation and generate a Notice without manual review, it is fast enough to issue that Notice promptly too.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Fairness to owners and the practical ability to verify or contest what the system has decided, both depend on closing this gap.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: When we tighten thresholds – a lower alcohol limit, a new offence for any trace of a controlled substance, wider automated detection – we will catch more people, not just more dangerous people.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Some of the newly caught will be genuinely reckless, others will be ordinary drivers who crossed a line that has simply moved, perhaps for the first time in years of otherwise safe driving.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: The Bill already accepts that first-time and repeat offenders are different.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: That is exactly why it sets a lower penalty for a first offence and a higher one for a repeat offence under the grievous hurt provisions.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: I ask the Ministry to extend that same thinking to how we respond to first-time offenders at the lower end, not only to how we sentence them.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Concretely, for first-time offenders caught under the newly tightened thresholds, go easy; pair a shorter suspension with mandatory retraining, such as a defensive driving or road safety course, so that the driver leaves with better habits, not merely a served suspension.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: For repeat offenders, go hard; the escalation the Bill already builds in for repeat conduct is right, and should stay uncompromising.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: A first-time, lower-culpability offender who completes retraining is less likely to re-offend than one who simply waits out a suspension and returns with the same habits unchanged.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: A repeat offender has already shown that leniency did not work and deserves the fuller weight of the law.

speaker: Mr Gabriel Lam (Sembawang)
text: Both would make it fairer and stronger in its execution.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: While Singapore has one of the lowest crime rates worldwide, our roads are becoming increasingly dangerous.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There is a Chinese phrase, "马路如虎口", which means the roads are like the mouths of tigers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We must not allow more innocent lives to be lost due to careless or reckless drivers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Hence, I support the amendments to the Road Traffic Bill, to impose stiffer penalties on dangerous and careless driving causing grievous hurt, specifically due to drink driving and using mobile communication devices while driving.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Smartphones have become an integral part of our lives because they remove most of the friction from everyday transactions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: They have also become a mobile platform for entertainment videos.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many people find it a struggle to leave their phones out of sight or not to use their smartphones for an extended duration of time or for doom scrolling, which to me, is a blight on modern life.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: But it is not just bad for our cognitive and social development – it is a dangerous habit for drivers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Instead of focusing their eyes and their minds on the road conditions, their attention is split between operating their cars and operating their smartphones.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Smartphones usage is a common cause of split-second misjudgement and mishandling of vehicles, resulting in accidents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In our densely-populated city-state with millions of road users daily, the probability and risks of one being involved in a serious road accident has been on the rise.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: So long the driver holds the mobile communication device in his or her hand while the vehicle is in motion, even if the driver is not making a call or typing a message, this would constitute an offence.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In contrast, if the device is mounted, it is not an offence.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: While the revised definition gives clarity to what constitutes an offence, it may not have necessarily addressed the real cause of distraction to the driver.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As a case in point, it is not an uncommon sight for drivers to be watching their Korean or Chinese dramas on their mounted smart devices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In reality, the driver's attention is clearly divided if his or her attention is on the characters inside the mobile phone screen, rather than on the other vehicles and pedestrians in front of his or her big windscreen.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: My concern is that instead of curtailing distracting activities related to the use of smart communication devices, the amendments may instead legitimatise the blatant misuse of mounted devices.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Over the years, the Traffic Police have installed hundreds of speed cameras, red-light cameras, set up roadblocks and deployed dozens of patrol teams to apprehend drivers who are speeding or drinking under the influence of alcohol.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Although resource-intensive, kudos to the hard work of the the Traffic Police officers, they have kept our roads relatively safe over the past decades.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The use of mobile communication devices while driving will be much harder to detect, let alone to apprehend the offenders red-handed with evidence.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Many vehicles have sunshades attached onto the windows and drivers may be operating their phones at a position well below eye-level, which makes it even harder to gather evidence.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, it would be difficult for the Traffic Police riders or patrol teams to detect someone operating their smart devices, let alone other members of public, unless they are sitting in the same vehicles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Hence, I am concerned over the efficacy of the latest amendments, other than to deter bad behaviour.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: My view is that other than stricter penalties, we need to work on three areas, namely instilling awareness, education and leveraging technology.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: First of all, we should instill awareness in our young children both in school and at home, to always be vigilant.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: It is a common sight these days of pedestrians looking down at their mobile phones, wearing headphones and looking completely oblivious to the surroundings, while crossing the roads.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These inattentive pedestrians are a hazard if they appear out of nowhere, especially at night at zebra crossings and at traffic lights crossings.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We need stronger measures to remind pedestrians not to use their mobile communication devices while crossing roadways.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Road Safety Park at East Coast Parkway has always been a fun and an effective way for primary school students to learn about traffic rules.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: However, the roadways these days have become more complicated.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Improved traffic lights systems, such as the Red Amber Green turning lights have been deployed in many cross junctions and curb cut crossings have also been added to help pedestrians cross roadways more safely.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The Road Safety Park should be revamped to incorporate the latest road safety features.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Students attending road safety course should also learn about the dangers of a pedestrian using mobile phones and wearing headphones playing loud music.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: If these poor habits are not corrected from a young age, it may be a lot harder to convince a teenager to stay vigilant and alert on the roads, until something bad happens.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Thirdly, drivers should leverage on technology to operate their mobile communication devices using voice activated commands.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: With software enhancements, most devices are now equipped with voice recognition functions, for instance, replying a WhatsApp message using voice instead of typing out the message.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: In case of an urgent need to make a call or reply to a message, drivers can use voice-activated commands, which will reduce the need to operate their mobile devices with their hands while driving.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: These measures should not only be directed at drivers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We should also cultivate awareness in our children from young, both in school and at home, so that they remain vigilant.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We need stronger measures to remind pedestrians not to use their mobile communication devices while crossing the road.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: As a society, every road user has a responsibility to practice road safety, to keep each other out of harm's way.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We should all take a proactive, preventative approach to minimise road accidents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Stiffer penalties can only be a deterrent because after an accident occurs, the harm and damage caused cannot be undone.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: We do not wish to live in regret that we should have been more vigilant and more careful.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Let us continue to remind one another that the roads will always remain dangerous unless every user does his or her part to stay safe.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: (In English): At the end of the day, safe driving boils down to a sense of responsibility and self-discipline.

text: Every driver should understand that their fast-moving vehicle can become a weapon that can destroy life and property.

text: They may also have to serve time in jail and lose their driving licence if found guilty.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: To focus on punitive measures and detection is akin to filling a leaking bucket.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: The best and perhaps the only solution is to stow away the smart devices when driving, especially if they are not required for navigation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: There are countries which ban devices for young children because of the damage to their minds.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang West)
text: Why do we do less for actions which damage our lives?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I think, importantly, it is hoped that over time, these amendments will enable all road users to reset driving habits and reshape road behaviours.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: And if we are able to achieve this, then our roads will be indeed safer for all.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I believe we can all agree that road safety affects more than just drivers and riders, whether we are pedestrians, public transport users, riders, cyclists or drivers at any given time.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: What is most concerning is the vulnerability of particular segments of our road users.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Fatal accidents involving elderly pedestrians more than doubled in one year from 11 in 2024 to 27 in 2025.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We also have recently read reports on the increase in work-related traffic fatalities and injuries.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Workers who travel on our roads daily for a living, such as our logistics and platform drivers and riders, face far greater risks due to increased exposure and time spent on the roads.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In many instances, they are involved in accidents not of their making but by the actions of other road users.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This Bill will hopefully go some way in addressing this and reducing these risks.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the past, for instance, a driver may attempt to evaluate how much he or she can drink to stay within the legal limit to drive.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: However, as we know, the effect of alcohol impairment, varies with gender, age, health and body composition.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: And with the proposed lower alcohol limit, the message is clearer: "If you drink, don't drive".

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, the Ministry, in its recent press release, made this statement that there is really no safe number of alcohol drinks before driving.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If this is the position that the Ministry takes, I thought I wanted to ask a question on whether the Minister can share if the Ministry considered a zero-tolerance stance like some jurisdictions have done with regards to alcohol limits and the reasons why the lower thresholds of alcohol limits were selected instead.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For the use of mobile devices, I think it is quite clear.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The amendments now clarify that if the vehicle is in motion, a driver should not, at any instance, be holding on to their mobile phones.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: There will be drivers who will say that they are holding on to their mobile phones is a matter of habit with no intention of use.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Others will say it is no difference from holding a cup of coffee while you are driving.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: But I would say that if this so, then, perhaps, it is a good opportunity to change the habit.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Holding a mobile phone in one hand inevitably gives rise to the possibility that the driver can and will be distracted by messages, by calls or even the temptation to scroll.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: With the proposed amendment, the message is now clear.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: When you drive, you either mount your device safely, integrate it with your vehicle's infotainment system.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For driving under the influence of drugs, the Bill seeks to remove the proof of impairment requirement, in cases where drivers are found under the influence of controlled drugs, psychoactive or intoxicating substances.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If a person is under such influence still chooses to drive and put other road users in danger, then the driver/rider must surely be taken to task by the law, without the onus being on the authorities to have to prove impairment.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, I would take a further step and ask if the Ministry will consider calibrating the exception for prescription drugs.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If a person is unwell and he is prescribed medications by his or her doctor that are not only likely, but it is almost certain to cause drowsiness or impairment, then the safe and responsible thing to do, must surely be – not to drive, not to ride.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Our officers no longer need to prove the use of a mobile phone while the vehicle is in operation.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: They do not need to prove impairment with the presence of controlled substances.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This is not a lowering or changing of standards.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It is the removal of evidential hurdles that make enforcement challenging.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Importantly, it will send an unambiguous and clear signal on where we stand as a society on road safety for all road users.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This Bill is not about new offences, higher thresholds or stiffer penalties.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It is about the driver who chooses to leave his or her car behind after a drink or the driver who remains fully focused on driving while leaving his mobile phone properly mounted on the dashboard.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Resetting driving habits and reshaping road behaviours are what this Bill seeks to achieve.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: And if we succeed, then perhaps, most of the provisions in this Bill may rarely have to be enforced at all.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We all want to return home safely to our families every day.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Safety on our roads is non-negotiable because behind every traffic fatality is a family for whom an ordinary everyday journey changed lives tragically and irreversibly.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Our roads are becoming less safe and I agree our laws must keep pace with changing behaviour and technology.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But whenever we expand criminal liability, we must also ensure that the law is clear, proportionate and fair.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Dangerous conduct should be punished, but ordinary drivers acting reasonably should not be unintentionally caught by the law.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Today, I wish to speak on three areas: the proposed offence of holding a mobile communication device while driving, the lowering of the drink driving limits and finally, road hogging.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: First, holding of mobile communication devices while driving.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I welcome the proposed amendment to section 65B.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is sensible that the Bill does not criminalise the holding or the use of a handphone while a vehicle is stationary.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It closes an evidential gap and makes enforcement easier.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But we must be careful not to replace one problem with another.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A phone may slip from its holder or fall near the pedals.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A driver may instinctively pick it up, place it somewhere safe without looking at the screen or operating any function on the phone.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If a driver handles a phone just for a second, solely to remove an immediate hazard and without causing distraction to himself, will that still amount to an offence?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Motorists should not have to wait until they receive demerit points or face prosecution before discovering where the legal boundary lies.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: After all, we do not automatically criminalise a driver who briefly picks up a fallen water bottle, wallet or another object.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If doing so results in careless or dangerous driving, the driver can already be prosecuted.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But simply holding the object, in itself, is not an offence.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I therefore hope the Minister can clarify section 95 of the Penal Code will apply in such a situation as I have described.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Next, there is also an issue of consistency.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A driver may spend several seconds typing on a mounted phone, entering a destination into a navigation system or repeatedly tapping a touchscreen while the vehicle is moving.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: That can be equally distracting as holding a phone.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If the intent of the law is to remove distraction for the better of road safety, should we not also consider criminalising the act of operating a mounted device while driving?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A tougher rule for handphone use whilst driving is justified because this is a significant source of distraction.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But the law should also distinguish between the deliberate use of a phone, versus a temporary movement of a phone purely for necessity.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It should also address the the safety issues of whether a phone is held on one hand versus when it is mounted.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Both methods ultimately cause distractions for the driver.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I hope the Government can clarify these boundaries so that motorists can understand exactly what the law requires.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I fully support stronger action against drink driving.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The message should be simple: if you drink, do not drive.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If Parliament lowers the legal threshold by more than half, then the science behind enforcement must be equally robust.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It allows the reading to be taken closer to the time of driving.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But convenience must never come at the expense of accuracy.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I therefore ask the Minister how the margin of error for such measurements will be addressed, especially for the readings at or just above the legal limit?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Will borderline readings require confirmation, for example, a second test?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Will there be prosecutorial discretion shown for measurements that are just slightly above the limit?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Will drivers be entitled to a second test if the reading is only marginally above the prescribed limit?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I would also appreciate the clarification on how these devices will be approved and independently validated.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Have they been tested under Singapore's operating conditions, including our temperature and humidity?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If the accuracy of a device is challenged at trial, will maintenance, calibration and error records be disclosed to the defence?

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Public confidence depends not only on tough laws, but also on the confidence that the evidence is accurate.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I hope the Government will consider making reliable self-testing devices more accessible to members of public.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Consumer breathalysers are already available, but their quality varies greatly.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The Government could certify approved models, publish a list of independently tested devices or encourage licensed premises, such as restaurants, bars and clubs, to make certified devices available to all patrons.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The safest choice remains not to drive after drinking.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But prevention should go hand in hand with enforcement.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: If we expect motorists to comply with much lower limits, we should also equip them to make responsible decisions before getting behind the wheel.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Whether or not these claims are scientifically valid, they may give certain motorists a false sense of confidence.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Clear public guidance will help to ensure that the motorists do not rely on misleading advertisements and instead make responsible action, decision not to drive if in doubt.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Every driver in Singapore knows exactly what I am talking about.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: A driver remains in the rightmost lane despite having ample opportunity to move left.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Drivers weave across the lanes, overtaking on the left or follow too closely.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: What begins as inconsiderate behaviour can quickly become a safety issue for everyone.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Road hogging does not excuse speeding, tailgating or dangerous driving.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Every motorist remains responsible for his own action.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But neither should we ignore the conduct that unnecessarily creates congestion, frustration and conflict on our roads.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The speed limit is not a licence to camp in the overtaking lane nor should any driver take it upon himself to decide how fast everyone else behind him should travel.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Once that manoeuvre is completed, drivers should return to the left whenever it is safe to do so.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: I recognise that our existing Road Traffic Rules already require slower vehicles to keep left and prohibit obstructing faster-moving traffic.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But the reality is that many motorists either do not understand these rules or simply ignore them.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: The existing framework has not created sufficient awareness or deterrence.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Road hogging is more than just an annoyance.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We need to stop road hogging today to make our roads safer.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: But as we strengthen our laws, we must also ensure they remain fair, proportionate and practical.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We should draw a clear line between dangerous conduct and momentary acts done in the interest of safety.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: We should match tougher drink driving laws with reliable science, accurate enforcement and stronger prevention.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: And we should finally give road hogging the attention it deserves.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Safer roads require drivers who are attentive, sober and considerate.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: Road safety is not only about how fast we drive.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: It is also about how responsibly we share the road.

speaker: Ms Diana Pang Li Yen (Marine Parade-Braddell Heights)
text: With these observations, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Every day, hundreds of thousands of Singaporeans entrust their safety to other road users: to the driver in the next lane, to the cyclist ahead, to the stranger crossing the road at dusk.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Road safety is, at its heart, a promise we make to one another.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We do not know the people we share the road with and yet, we depend entirely on their care for us, as they depend on ours.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill states plainly, that the safety of one Singaporean can never be a lesser priority than the convenience of another.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some may ask whether this is too strict a standard.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A driver's reaction time is not a matter of personal preference – it is a matter of other people's lives.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A car travelling at 60 km/h covers almost 17 metres every second.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That is the difference between an elderly pedestrian safely crossing the road, and a family receiving a call no family should ever receive.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If a lower limit gives a driver even half a second more clarity, half a second more control, then it has already justified itself.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I support this change because it reflects a simple truth: the right to drive after drinking is not a matter of legal rights, but a risk that other road users were made to bear without their consent.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill returns that risk to where it belongs – with the driver who chose to take it.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, clause 10 and its enacted changes to mobile phone offences.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Devices must be properly secured to an approved mount.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I would gently suggest that we ask a different question: is the two seconds it takes to glance at a screen worth the safety risks it presents?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A driver's hands should hold a steering wheel, not a phone.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is not a difficult standard to meet and I believe most Singaporean drivers already meet it.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This amendment closes a loophole that allowed a driver to hold a phone at the wheel so long as they claimed that they were not using it.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Third, on clauses 6 to 8, and 21 and its changes to punitive and legal measures.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A driver who deliberately turns a vehicle into an instrument to frighten or harm another person has stepped outside the ordinary risks of the road and the law is right to treat that conduct with the seriousness it deserves.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Likewise, raising sentences for grievous hurt caused by dangerous driving sends an unambiguous signal: carelessness that maims or kills a fellow citizen is not merely a traffic matter – it is a matter of justice.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But, Sir, I wish to speak candidly on the introduction in of an automated decision-making system in clause 81A of the Bill, in the case of enforcement using a computer program.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Technology can help us process the sheer volume of footage and evidence that a modern transport system, like ours, generates and I do not doubt its usefulness.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I would urge this House and the Ministry, to hold firmly to one principle as we proceed: the law exists to serve people, not the other way around.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A computer program may assess evidence efficiently, but it cannot exercise judgement, cannot weigh context and cannot look a citizen in the eye.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is a difference between using technology to assist enforcement and allowing technology to become an arbiter of guilt.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Clause 2.7 of the Infocomm Media Development Authority Model AI Governance Framework posits the guiding principles that AI use in decision-making should be explainable, transparent, fair and human-centric.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will a human being review the assessment made by the system before a Notice is issued?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How will we ensure that we are not wrongly issuing Notices?

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A wrongly issued Notice imposes a heavy burden on those who do not know how to navigate the system or those with less bandwidth in their lives, such as delivery riders, who are already trying to work three jobs at a time.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must never let efficiency become a substitute for justice.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But, Sir, a safeguard that exists today must not erode over time.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I would ask the Ministry for an assurance.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This right should not exist only at the Bill's passage, but that it must be actively upheld, resourced and protected against dilution by future policy or operational shifts made without this House's scrutiny.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whatever tools we adopt to keep our roads safe, the citizen must remain at the centre of our legal system – not the algorithm, not the camera and not the convenience of the system.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: That principle must be non-negotiable today, and in every year that follows.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These behaviors are not befitting of who we say we are.

speaker: Ms Elysa Chen (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not only through the force of law, but through kind and socially-responsible decisions each of us makes every day.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Some time ago, my husband became concerned about my safety when I was driving.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: He helped me activate the "Do Not Disturb While Driving" function on my phone.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: When the phone detects that I may be driving, notifications are silenced and an automatic response can let others know that I am on the road.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: What struck me was that my husband did not simply tell me to exercise more self-control.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: He changed the settings around me, so that exercising self-control became easier.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Most drivers know that checking a phone while driving is dangerous.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: We tell ourselves that it will take only one second, or that we are good at multi-tasking.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Our devices are very effective at capturing our attention.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: They create a sense of urgency even when the message itself is not urgent.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: So, while individual responsibility must remain at the centre of road safety, we should also design systems that make responsible behaviour easier.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The Bill's focus on handheld devices is supported by evidence.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This makes sense when we consider the different ways in which a phone distracts us.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: There is visual distraction, when our eyes leave the road; physical distraction, when a hand leaves the steering wheel; cognitive distraction, when our mind is occupied by another task; and auditory distraction, when a sound or conversation draws our attention away.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Handheld phone use could potentially involve all four forms of distraction at the same time.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: This is why removing the need to prove that the driver was actively operating the device is a sensible amendment.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Deterrence depends not only on the severity of a penalty, but also on whether people believe that a violation is likely to be detected.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: However, the fact that the Bill does not prohibit mounted devices should not be taken to mean that they are necessarily safe.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A mounted device may remove the need to hold the phone, but it does not remove visual or cognitive distraction.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Mounted devices are also necessary for many drivers.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: Private hire, taxi and delivery drivers rely on phones for navigation and work allocation.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: The law must draw an enforceable line, but drivers should not mistake that legal line for the boundary between safe and unsafe behaviour.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: A phone mount is not a licence to multi-task.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: At the heart of this issue is the psychology of attention.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: What we casually call multi-tasking is in fact our attention switching rapidly between tasks.

speaker: Dr Charlene Chen (Tampines)
text: During each switch, we may fail to process important information.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I rise in support of this Bill, and my speech today will focus on specific issues and seek a few clarifications.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is not contentious that a driver should be punished under the present un-amended section 65B if he or she has used "the mobile communication device's communicative or other functions", since such a driver's attention is clearly divided and distracted from operating the vehicle safely.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The present section 65B rightly targets the impermissible policy object, which is the risk, if not the fact of distraction arising from the use of the device.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: That said, in a Mothership report dated 10 July 2026, MHA is cited as having clarified, and I quote, that "the acts of eating, drinking or smoking while driving are not offences in and of themselves".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Furthermore, on a close reading of the proposed amendment to section 65B, holding anything other than a "mobile communication device" as defined under section 65B(3) would not constitute an offence.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Ministry has described its approach as a "calibrated" one.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Could the Ministry explain how, in the context of the mere physical act of holding an object, it distinguishes between a mobile communication device on the one hand and everything else on the other?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To be clear, I am not proposing that eating, driving or smoking while driving should be criminalised.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, the Ministry's rationalisation of its calibrated approach should be clarified, especially since Parliament's intent will be examined by the enforcement authorities, legal practitioners and our Courts if the Bill is passed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My next clarification is whether the Ministry has contemplated specific scenarios in which drivers may inadvertently fall foul of the new section 65B.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And if the matter is left to police discretion, how should that discretion be exercised?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, even when a mobile communication device is properly secured in a mounting affixed in the manner intended by the manufacturer, it is not uncommon for such mounts to become dislodged.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This could be due to prolonged exposure to heat from Singapore's tropical climate as such mounts are most commonly affixed to the windshield of a vehicle under direct sunlight or due to hard braking or other maneuver to avoid an accident.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And just as what my fellow Parliamentary colleague, Ms Diana Pang, has shared earlier, it is not a fanciful possibility that a driver may instinctively catch a falling device and at that precise moment, be observed by the Police.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another plausible scenario involves private hire car or other driving service providers who need to plug in a hands-free earpiece to take a call, especially when it is not practicable for them to use the vehicle's built-in Bluetooth function for privacy reasons or to minimise the disturbance caused to their passenger.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My other clarification under this clause is to seek the rationale behind the Ministry's proposal to remove the "operate" element entirely, rather than, for example, requiring a driver alleged to have committed an offence under the new section 65B to prove on a balance of probabilities that he or she was not operating a device.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In my view, the latter would be a more calibrated approach than what is currently proposed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I now turn to the question of how we can keep rehabilitation and the protection of livelihoods in view as we strengthen our road safety framework.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just as what my fellow Parliamentary colleague, Ms Poh Li San has shared with this House earlier, as the Chinese saying goes, "马路如虎口".

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The road is just like a tiger's mouth.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Yet, as many of my hon colleagues and I have encountered on a regular basis at our respective Meet-the-People Sessions, we must not forget that many residents rely on their driving licence to earn a living and raise their families.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While we strengthen enforcement and enhance penalties for errant road users, I sincerely believe that there must also be room for second chances.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
