text: What I mean is this: especially for private hire car drivers, delivery drivers, passenger-ferrying drivers and others whose livelihoods are wholly dependent on operating a vehicle, could they, instead of or prior to suspension, be placed on a driving performance improvement plan, just like what my Parliamentary colleague, Mr Darryl David, has also suggested in his speech earlier, and/or consider for these drivers to be allowed to provide a sum with sufficient deterrent effect to guarantee good driving behaviour, similar to the concept of a bail?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Save for those disqualified for life, other drivers have the prospect of returning as responsible road users.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This proposal, I believe, could rehabilitate these motorists more effectively and more quickly for their personal betterment and for greater utility to the public.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: These motorists would also realise, if they had not already, the grave consequences of continued errant driving; namely, loss of their driving licence, consequent loss of livelihood, financial hardship for themselves and their families and most importantly, that it is entirely within their control to avoid these outcomes.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The core policy objective of safer roads would remain unchanged.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The signal would, if anything, be strengthened; that bad behaviour attracts real consequences.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This, to me, is another calibrated approach that would further our goal of improving safety while allowing drivers and perhaps also their families, a second chance to avoid ending up in a perilous and potentially unrecoverable situation.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: My next point concerns ensuring that every affected driver charged in Court has access to justice.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In Mandarin): Mr Deputy Speaker, while this Bill rightly focuses on strengthening the responsibilities of drivers, road safety is ultimately a shared duty.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If the fundamental aim of this Bill is to enhance overall road safety, then a more holistic approach, one that also encourages all road users to stay vigilant would further strengthen that objective. : Notwithstanding my above clarifications and suggestions, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: However, enforcement cannot be the sole problem solver or the whole answer.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: As is often the case, we must also go upstream.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Today, I will cover three points: disproportionate impact of fines on the vulnerable, using data to identify patterns; but first, Singapore's road culture.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The wider consideration is the culture on our roads.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The issue cannot be a lack of knowledge.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It also should not be impatience, distraction and a lack of consideration for other road users.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: First, how will MHA and the Traffic Police work with driving schools and private instructors to review the driving curriculum and on-the-road tests.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Learning to drive should not only be about passing the theory and practical tests.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: There should be greater emphasis on defensive driving and road courtesy.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A learner driver should understand the risks of scrolling on the phone, tailgating or accelerating towards a junction or when the light is changing or when someone signals.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It is about ensuring they understand the responsibility that comes with being in control of a vehicle.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Second, education should not stop once a person obtains a license.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Where a driver repeatedly commits traffic offences, there may be value in requiring that person to attend a refresher or corrective driving course.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For some offenders, a fine is paid and then forgotten.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A good corrective course may have a more lasting effect.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The offender will have to confront driving habits, understand risks created and learn how to respond differently.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The objective should go beyond punishing the offence that has already happened but also preventing the next offence.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Third, the data collected through automated enforcement should be used to identify patterns.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For example, if many motorists are speeding along the same road, running a red light at the same junction or committing the same offence at the same location, we should ask why and what are the factors beyond poor driving behaviours?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Perhaps, it is road design, signage or traffic-light timing?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I urge the Traffic Police and LTA to use, track and share data on its findings and the changes it plans to make to the road environment in an attempt to reduce the risk of offences and accidents.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A resident may not dispute the offence nor the fine but seeks help no less because he or she is struggling to pay it.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We unpacked and explored some solutions, including reaching out to social service agencies and also Malay/Muslim organisations.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Mr X's case is of course not the only one.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: When the driver is a sole breadwinner managing bills, arrears and other family expenses, the fine can be the straw that breaks the camel's back.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We therefore should ask: how are fines actually punishing lower-income offenders more heavily than better-off offenders?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A $500 fine is the same amount for everyone.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For a higher-income driver, it may be an inconvenience – cutting back spending for the month.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For a lower-income worker, the same fine may mean having to go a little hungrier, a room that is a little dimmer or postponing the doctor's appointment.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: A person's income cannot determine whether he or she is required to obey traffic laws but how do we mitigate the impact to the vulnerable?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Under such a system, the seriousness of the offence determines the scale of the penalty while the offender's income determines the actual amount payable.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I recognise this will not be straightforward to introduce in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: There will definitely be legitimate questions about how income should be assessed.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It would be useful to understand whether fixed fines achieve a broadly similar deterrent effect across different income groups or whether they are too easily absorbed by some and disproportionately damaging to others.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In the meantime, there are practical measures that can be considered.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: An applicant could be required to provide supporting documents, and serious and, of course, repeat offenders could be excluded.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: By this way, a reasonable instalment plan may prevent a one-off offence from creating a much larger financial crisis for the offender's family.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Importantly, the fine would still have to be paid and the person would still be held accountable.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For suitable lower-level offences, MHA could also consider corrective driving courses or corrective work orders to be imposed alongside or in limited cases instead of part of the financial penalty.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: This should not apply to drink driving, deliberate dangerous driving, repeat offending or conduct causing grievous hurt.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: But for less serious offences, we should ask whether a financial penalty is always the best way to change behaviours.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The point is not to be soft on offenders.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It is to make sure the penalty works.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: As the Member of Parliament Dr Wan Rizal mentioned earlier, road safety is more than just law enforcement – it also depends on understanding and education.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I would also suggest that the Government work together with social service agencies, as well as Malay/Muslim organisations, to ensure that road users understand these amendments and feel assured, so that they will comply going forward.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Yet, its value and impact can sometimes be vastly different.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For a high-income driver, it may be little more than a minor inconvenience.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: But for a lower-income worker, that same fine may mean tightening one's belt, unpaid bills and mounting debt.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: So, are we, in effect, punishing the less well-off more heavily than those with higher income?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I wish to be clear that one's financial situation does not excuse dangerous driving.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Salary or income should not determine whether a person is required to obey traffic laws.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: However, there are countries that employ a system of income-based fines.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The purpose is to ensure that fines carry a meaningful deterrent effect.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I recognise this would not be straightforward to introduce in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For instance, a person may have a low salary but possess substantial assets.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: But could MHA at least explore if this proposal can be considered?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: In the meantime, there are several practical measures that can be considered.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Of course, applications need not be approved indiscriminately, and applicants should certainly be required to provide strong and genuine supporting evidence.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The point is not to be soft on offenders.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Rather, the objective is to ensure that the penalty can be truly effective without jeopardising the offender's family stability. : Mr Deputy Speaker, safer roads will not come from higher penalties alone.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singapore needs better drivers, better training, earlier interventions, safer road design, sensible use of technology and a fair approach to financial penalties.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It should shape society's conduct, earn public confidence and strengthen our values that holds Singapore together.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But I would like to make one broader point.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Deterrence is necessary, but deterrence must ultimately culminate in prevention.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The best outcome is not that we punish a dangerous driver more severely after an accident.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is that we use stronger laws, better technology and better information to prevent that accident from happening in the first place.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I welcome the tightening of the drink driving and drug driving regime.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I had previously asked a Parliamentary Question on protocols for road traffic offences involving drugs and asked for stricter penalties.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: While drink driving rightly receives significant attention, drug-impaired driving can also have devastating consequences.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And I am glad that the Ministry is now implementing stricter protocols and stiffer penalties for both.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: If we want better prevention, we need better understanding.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The data should tell us where enforcement and education can have the greatest impact.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I welcome the amendments allowing the Traffic Police to use automated decision-making for objectively verifiable offences, such as speeding and red light violations.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: The Bill also allows photographic and video evidence submitted by members of the public to be used for the mobile device offence.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Technology should not merely help us process more offences.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Some time ago, I filed a Parliamentary Question regarding accidents and traffic enforcement cameras along Loyang Avenue, after residents repeatedly raised concerns about speeding and dangerous driving.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At that time, I was informed that camera deployment was not practical due to space constraints.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: On that note, I am really grateful for LTA for the measures that they have put there, but I hope MHA can invest in technology and AI to overcome the technical limitations we have for our current camera systems.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It should also help us see danger coming.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This is also why I support greater use of citizen reporting.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Many residents submit videos or pictures of dangerous driving or illegal parking through LTA's OneMotoring platform.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And could better feedback be provided to those who take the effort to submit evidence?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: People are more willing to participate when they know their contribution makes a difference.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, as we give the Traffic Police greater ability to leverage on technology, I urge the Ministry to also look at how accident data, traffic violations and citizen reports can be used to identify emerging hotspots.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: My next point, prevention is not only about the driver.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It is also about the road environment and the organisations operating on our roads.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Residents have raised concerns about Pasir Ris Drive 3.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In May this year, a cyclist tragically lost her life following a collision involving a tipper truck.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Along Tanah Merah Coast Road, cyclists have also raised concerns about loose gravel, debris, accumulated dirt and stationary heavy vehicles along cycling paths.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: When they move onto the road because the cycling path is unsafe, we should not immediately assume that they are simply being irresponsible.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Sometimes, the safer choice is just not available.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Enforcing matters pertaining to heavy vehicles involve several agencies – the Traffic Police, LTA and NEA – with different responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: They see gravel falling from trucks, they see debris accumulating and they see cycling paths becoming unsafe.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: So, where repeated breaches create persistent hazards, could enforcement, road maintenance and action against recurring sources of debris be better coordinated?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: There is also a question of corporate responsibility.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Where an individual driver commits an offence, that driver should be held accountable.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: But if the same operator or company repeatedly has vehicles associated with unsafe driving, poorly secured loads or other safety breaches, should we not also ask whether there is a deeper management problem?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Could persistent safety breaches by operators be met with stronger licensing or operational consequences where appropriate?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Road safety should not end with the person behind the wheel.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: It should also be part of the organisation's safety culture.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For drivers returning after lengthy disqualification, could the Ministry consider a structured refresher or a rehabilitation programme before their licences are restored?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: A driving test demonstrates competence at that moment in time, but not necessarily judgement or changed attitudes.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: We should ensure that those returning to our roads are ready not just to drive, but to drive responsibly.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And in my latest morning ride with some members from the Safety for Active Mobility Users, I learnt about a simple framework that captures this – the MAS framework.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Not Meet-the-People Session, but MAS. "M" for mentality: the most important one in their opinion, to recognise that another person's safety is more important than our own convenience. "A" for awareness: stay alert, slow down and anticipate others.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: And "S" for skill: stay in control and respond safely when situations change.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: I support the Bill and look forward to the Ministry's reply.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When the question of lane splitting was previously shared in this House, the Ministry's position was that an outright ban is impractical and difficult to enforce.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Instead, the Government's approach relies on a catch-all charge for dangerous or careless driving, the principle of shared responsibility among all road users and safety mandates, such as anti-lock braking systems on new motorcycles.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I do not dispute that enforcing a specific ban presents real difficulties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, given that motorcyclist fatalities and serious accidents remain disproportionately high, I strongly urge that public education on safe riding practices be stepped up urgently, including clear messaging that lane splitting can amount to careless and dangerous behaviour.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In terms of public education, can we also extend it to foreign-registered vehicles and motorcyclists, such as by sending SMS reminders to all LTA Vehicle Entry Permit-holders, and putting up reminders at strategic locations, such as at the ICA premises at the Causeway?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My second question concerns Ministry's views on ensuring that both hands are on the wheel when driving.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We all know that both hands must be on the steering wheel when operating motor vehicles, but very often, we see drivers with one hand on the wheel, while the other hand is tapping or scrolling on the phone, on a mounted device or holding a cigarette.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This involves visual and manual disengagement from the wheel in ways similar to device use.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My third question is regarding the Traffic Police's deployment of Traffic Violation Enforcement Cameras (TVECs).

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could the Ministry share more about these plans?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, I seek clarification on whether these TVECs detect drivers' failures to signal and insufficient durations during signalling for lane changes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is an issue that my residents and many drivers have been giving feedback on, in view of a worsening trend.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How often might TVECs be redeployed, especially in high-risk areas?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would also urge the Ministry to step up enforcement against dangerous behaviours by other road users, including motorists who do not slow down when approaching pedestrian crossings and tapping on technology for identification of offenders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My last question is on protecting our seniors at pedestrian crossings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other jurisdictions have adopted hybrid crossing models with encouraging results.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin): My last question is on protecting our seniors at pedestrian crossings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Other jurisdictions have adopted hybrid crossing models with encouraging results.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The UK's crossing pairs zebra markings with a signal cycle legally compels vehicles to stop; its new crossing goes further, using sensors to hold the signal red for exactly as long as a slower-moving pedestrian needs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Ministry consider studying these cases for converting our higher-risk, unsignalised crossings in School Zones or Silver Zones to such models? : Sir, it is the responsibility of all road users to play their parts in road safety.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our road traffic framework and system must empower each to do so.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the Ministry will continue to treat both the calibration of our rules and the evidence behind them with equal rigour, so that when a rider, driver or elderly resident places their trust in the system, that trust is backed by the assurance for their safety.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Whether we are drivers, cyclists or pedestrians, we all expect our roads to be safe.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Every accident prevented means a life protected and a family spared from tragedy.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome these amendments because our roads are changing.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Traffic is increasing, technology is evolving and our laws must keep pace.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The law should rightly distinguish between careless driving and deliberate acts of violence.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Second, I welcome the stronger measures against drink and drug driving.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Third, I support the greater use of technology in enforcement.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Computer-assisted systems can improve efficiency and consistency, provided there is proper human oversight.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: The success of this Bill should not be measured by the number of summonses issued, but whether it changes behaviour.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: They will learn about these changes through public education and the media, or maybe one day, when they receive the summonses themselves.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: That is why implementation is just as important as legislation.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Ministry will roll out a strong public education campaign to explain what has changed, why the changes are needed and what motorists need to do differently.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister also consider a clearly communicated transition period for amendments that introduce new obligations?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Serious offences, such as dangerous driving, drink or drug driving and excessive speeding, should continue to be dealt firmly.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: It is about giving the public a fair opportunity to understand the new requirements before full enforcement begins.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister share how these systems will be monitored?

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: Effective enforcement must be fair and trusted and lasting behavioural change requires education to go hand in hand with enforcement.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: If we get this balance right, we will achieve what we all want: safer roads, more responsible motorists and greater public confidence in our road traffic laws.

speaker: Mr Jackson Lam (Nee Soon)
text: With those remarks, Sir, I support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I rise in support of the Road Traffic (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill strengthens our response to dangerous driving.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It better distinguishes deliberate harm from negligence, strengthens deterrence against the most serious offending and makes enforcement more effective through technology.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Every one of them started the day expecting to return home.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For those who survived with serious injuries, the accident is often only the beginning.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is why, while I support the Bill, I hope to raise four issues where I believe we can strengthen its impact: ensuring automated enforcement remains accessible and fair; helping patients understand the implications of prescribed medications; designing safer roads for an ageing population; and recognising the lifelong consequences of permanent neurological injury.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, on the automated decision-making system for camera-detected offences.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The efficiency gains are real, given the huge number of violations the Traffic Police has to process a year.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But removing manual review for even objectively verifiable offences, like speeding, places greater weight on the appeal process.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Minister share what safeguards will ensure the 14-day appeal window is genuinely accessible to elderly or less digitally literate vehicle owners?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, I have questions regarding the new offence of driving with controlled or psychoactive substances present in blood, regardless of impairment.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While this is a reasonable deterrent, it depends on drivers knowing which common medications could trigger liability.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Ministry commit to a public education campaign, in partnership with pharmacies and general practitioners so that patients on legitimate prescriptions are not caught unaware?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Two groups stand out, both in the statistics and in the patients I have treated.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They simply experience the road differently, needing more time to cross safely.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As Singapore ages, and as new towns, like Tengah, take shape, I hope the Ministry will consider whether roads can be designed around how people actually move, rather than assuming uniformed walking speeds.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Residents' requests for safer crossings are also valuable information about how they actually use their neighbourhoods.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope the Ministry will consider whether this information can be used earlier in new towns to guide where crossing improvements are most needed.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin): At this point, I would like to say a few words on behalf of our senior residents.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is not that they disregard the rules or do not value their own safety.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope road designs can take greater account of how residents of different ages and abilities use our roads. : Motorcyclists are the second group.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A serious accident can affect not only their livelihood, but also the families who depend on them.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Could the Minister update the House on the timeline for mandatory rider refresher training and whether technologies that have improved safety for other vehicle classes could be extended to motorcycles?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One sentence in the Explanatory Statement describes traumatic brain injury resulting in a permanent vegetative state as "almost as serious as death".

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many people imagine recovery as a period of rest followed by a return to normal life.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Recovery, when it happens, unfolds over months and years.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Others improve only to a certain point despite the best efforts of the patient, family and rehabilitation team.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The difficulty is not only that recovery takes time.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is that the person's life and the family's life, may never return to what it once was.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is why I ask whether permanent and irreversible neurological impairment could be recognised as a distinct aggravating factor in sentencing and whether the Government is reviewing longer-term rehabilitation and caregiver support for affected families.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Such support would complement, not compete with, this Bill's deterrent aims.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A family well-supported through recovery is also a family better able to see justice served without being consumed by it.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Working in rehabilitation has taught me that the consequences of a road accident do not end when the ambulance leaves.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For some families, the consequences last a lifetime.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: That is why I hope we continue to judge our road safety system not only by how firmly it punishes dangerous driving, but also by how many Singaporeans never need rehabilitation because the accident never happened.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: I would first declare my role as one of the advisors to the National Taxi Association.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: These figures represent real lives lost and families shattered.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: A split second is all it takes – a split second of distraction, a split second of eyes off the road and a life is changed forever.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: This is a critical turning point to zero in on the reckless behaviour endangering our streets.

speaker: Ms Lee Hui Ying (Nee Soon)
text: While I understand this is intended to simplify enforcement and allow for camera-based detection, there are some practical questions that I hope the Minister and Ministry can clarify.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: While this Bill strengthens our law, punishment is ultimately the last line of defence.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Deterrence depends on severity of punishment but certainty of detection, the speed and consistency of enforcement matters.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, for the purpose of this Bill, I will focus on three specific areas: number one, distracted driving; number two, drink driving and impaired driving; number three, the use of technology in enforcement.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, the amendment Bill recognises that it is an offence for driver to hold a mobile communication device when his or her vehicle in moving.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is no longer necessary to establish that the driver was operating on one of the device functions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill also clarifies that touching a device properly secured and mounting does not constitute holding it.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I support this change because the driver holding a phone or another communication device may already be distracted even if it is difficult to prove whether he or she was typing, making a call or using a particular mobile app.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, this means that enforcement will be more practical in this regard.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: MHA has also stated that the offence may be enforced using camera and photographic or video evidence submitted by members of public.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Back to the idea I mentioned earlier on certainty of detection, could the Ministry clarify whether the Traffic Police will publish guidance on the minimum information and quality of evidence for public submission?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is important because as a parent and as a Member of Parliament, I know residents who witnessed dangerous driver behaviour often want to do their part, but they need to know what can be reported, what evidence is exactly useful, how to submit without putting himself at risk?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Specifically, would a photograph or a video showing a driver holding a device with vehicle registration number be sufficient?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If a witness can provide vehicle number, location and time but the recording is not sufficiently clear, would the Police also consider checking with other available camera footage to corroborate the report?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Clear guidance would help members of public to make reports that can be acted upon.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill also draws a distinction between holding a device and touching one that is secured in mounting.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This distinction is understandable, but distraction does not disappear simply because the phone is being mounted.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A driver may still spend extended period of time typing, reading messages, scrolling through manuals and entering direction when vehicle is moving.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, could the Minister therefore clarify how this provision will work together and whether the Traffic Police will issue practical guidance in future when interaction with a mounted device may cross into the line of careless or dangerous driving?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I support a firm approach to drink driving.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The public message should be simple: if a person intends to drink, he or she should not drive, full stop.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Similar to what Minister Sim Ann mentioned earlier, motorists should not treat the new limit as an allowance or an attempt to calculate how many drinks they may consume just to remain below it because the effect of alcohol varies across different factors, such as body composition, health, food consumption and medication.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill also creates an offence when a controlled drug, psychoactive substance or intoxicating substance is present in a driver's blood.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Unlike general offence of impaired driving, the provision applies based on the presence of specific substances, regardless of the quantity detected, without the need to prove the observed impairment.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill provides a defence where a substance was lawfully consumed or administered, that the driver did not know or have reason to believe that it will affect his or her ability to control the vehicle.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How would the ordinary person taking medication lawfully, understand this obligation?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For many of us who are taking prescribed medication at some point, he or she is just following the doctor's instruction and he or she should not need to have specialised legal knowledge to understand whether how it may affect their driving.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: So, the term "specific substance" does cover a broad category under several pieces of legislation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It is not presented to the motorists as a simple list of medicine or substance.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My ask is whether would MHA work with the Ministry of Health (MOH), doctors and pharmacists and medicine suppliers to provide clear guidelines on commonly prescribed or dispensed medicine that fall within this provision.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Will medication labels and patient advice be strengthened where a medicine may affect driving?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The guidance should be clear and publicly available before provision comes into force.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, the Bill allows the Deputy Commissioner of Police to authorise the use of computer program to access recorded images or video.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Where the program assesses that there is sufficient evidence of a prescribed offence, it may cause a notice to be issued requiring a vehicle owner to identify the driver.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I support the use of technology to process straightforward cases more quickly to free officers for work that requires human judgement.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Separately, Government has also announced that the Driver Improvement Points System will be tightened from 1 January 2027.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Given the punitive framework, it is already being strengthened.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A person may apply for a notice to be revoked on the basis that the vehicle was not at the location of the alleged offence.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The evidence then will be reviewed by the Deputy Commissioner or an authorised public officer who will confirm or revoke the notice?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Whether the system uses AI or any other form of automated analysis, people must be able to check the evidence behind its conclusion.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Just as today we tell all citizens to not just trust what AI produce, you have to fact check.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Likewise, we must also allow people to check when an offence is being issued.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But criminal enforcement, in my view, is the last line of defence after dangerous conduct has already occurred.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Road safety responsibility, therefore, cannot be the responsibility of MHA and Traffic Police alone.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: MHA and Traffic Police are responsible for laws and enforcement.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Ministry of Transport and LTA shape our roads, our junctions, our crossings, speed limits and traffic calming measures.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The Ministry of Education and our schools continue to teach our children to be safe road users, and hopefully, the children will go back home to discuss this at home as well with their families.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: MOH and healthcare professions have an important role in ensuring that patients understand whether medication affects their ability to drive.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Even at local level, People's Association and other community partners play an important role in identifying recurring danger sports, gather resident feedback, bring road safety education to families and seniors.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because in my view, if we are serious about building a Singapore made for families, then road safety must be treated as a family policy.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A child should be able to cross the road outside the school safely.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: A senior should be able to walk to the market with confidence.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is the kind of Singapore I want my children and my family to be able to grow up in, one that they can move safely.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Most countries were asking how to reduce the number, but Sweden asked: what if we refuse to accept any road death as inevitable?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That became Vision Zero, adopted by their Parliament in 1997.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While Singapore should not import another country's model wholesale, its central insight travels well: human error is inevitable, but our transport system should be designed so that those mistakes are less likely to become tragedies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is a useful lens for this Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For many years, road safety focused mainly on the driver, who remains responsible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Modern road safety, however, is also shaped by platform algorithms, vehicle-sharing, medication risks and automated enforcement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As risks become more interconnected, responsibility must be shared.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It strengthens deterrence, modernises enforcement and closes gaps.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I will raise five areas where we can build a safer, more trusted road system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, a vehicle must never become a weapon.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There is a clear moral and legal difference between a lapse, reckless driving and deliberately using a vehicle to terrorise another person.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, what would ordinarily amount to the "special reasons" needed to depart from lifetime disqualification?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, how will the forfeiture operate when the vehicle belongs to an unknowing employer, rental company, car-sharing operator, or family member?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The law should punish the person who weaponises the vehicle while protecting an owner who neither knew of nor consented to the conduct.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When anger turns a vehicle into a weapon, the law must draw a line as firm as the harm is grave.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It also targets specified substances in a driver's blood, permits passive breath testing and modernises procedures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I support this firm stance; the message should be simple: if you drink, do not drive.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But as our population ages, the next frontier in impaired driving may not be alcohol alone, but lawful medication.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many older residents take several prescribed medicines daily for pain, insomnia, anxiety, or chronic conditions, and understandably, assume that any prescribed medicine is safe for driving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill provides a statutory defence for lawful, unknowing consumption, but a legal defence raised after investigation is a poor substitute for prevention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will MHA, MOH or Health Sciences Authority jointly issue a plain language guide on the new limits, specified substances, and testing procedures?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will healthcare professionals receive standard guidance on advising patients whose medication may affect driving?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I propose a recognisable, prominent national "Do Not Drive" symbol for medicines presenting a material driving risk.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: HealthHub could also provide a checker explaining whether a prescribed medicine affects driving, what precautions to take and when to seek advice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially important for vocational drivers whose livelihoods depend on the road.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Government should work with operators, unions and healthcare providers to offer short refresher modules whenever major traffic rules change.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The hallmark of good legislation is not that it expects ordinary people to be perfect, but that it helps them make better decisions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The best prosecution is the one that never becomes necessary.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, the Bill sharpens the offence concerning mobile communication devices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will no longer be necessary to prove that a driver holding a device was also operating its functions and it clarifies that touching a properly mounted device does not amount to holding it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For many taxi, private hire and delivery drivers, however, the mounted phone is not merely a telephone.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is their workplace, constantly providing navigation, ride requests, delivery assignments, customer messages and payment alerts.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Drivers must remain responsible, but platforms also shape behaviour.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If a platform can dictate how quickly a driver responds, how jobs are queued, or penalising a non-responsive driver, it has the power to design systems that support safer attention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could non-essential notifications be suppressed while a vehicle is moving?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could drivers receive longer response windows, use more voice-enabled functions, or have apps default to a simplified driving mode once vehicular movement is detected?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While auto-accept reduces tapping, if drivers still have only seconds to reject an unsuitable job, the pressure to look down remains.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is especially critical for private hire drivers who spend long hours on the road, often switching between multiple apps simultaneously.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This does not prevent innovation; it directs it toward safety.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a sensible use of automation to improve speed, consistency, and free up officers for complex work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill also provides an important safeguard, allowing recipients to seek a revocation that triggers human review.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To be precise, the program does not convict anyone; it initiates an information requirement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Failure to do so is an offence, and for certain offences, a licensed owner is presumed to have been driving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When automation triggers such legal duties, transparency and human review must be absolute.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, notices triggered by automated detection must clearly state that they were generated by an AI system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, notices should provide easy digital access to the visual evidence, location, timestamp, vehicle details and a plain language explanation of the suspected offence.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, the review process should accommodate material errors beyond the Bill's express grounds, such as misread plates, lane confusion, or other clear signs of a wrongly issued notice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The most revealing measure is not simply how often the system is right, but how it detects, corrects and learns when it is wrong.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The governing principles should be straightforward: transparency, explainability, meaningful human oversight, auditability and continuous improvement.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A computer may issue the first notice, but it must never have the final word.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When the state automates enforcement, it must make human accountability just as robust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Enforcement agencies need to identify drivers swiftly, and proper records to prevent evasion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Not every organisation is a major logistics operator with a fleet management system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many small and medium companies own only one or two vans shared among employees, and charities use vehicles to deliver meals or equipment using rotating volunteers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Since the law mandates collecting and retaining sensitive personal details, the Government must also help these organisations protect that data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will the implementation guidance address access controls, secure storage, safe disposal and general data-protection obligations?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There should also be a reasonable transition period, where genuine administrative errors are distinguished from deliberate concealments or the falsification of records.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Good regulation is not measured by the paperwork it generates, but by how effectively it solves problems and how safely it handles sensitive data.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many focus on the word "zero", an unpragmatic promise that no one would ever die on the roads.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I think the critical word here is "vision", a decision about the deaths a society refuses to accept.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is the spirit behind the five areas I spoke on: purposeful endangerment, impaired driving, digital distraction, automated enforcement and record keeping.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While these may look like separate issues, they point in a single direction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For decades, road safety policy asked how to change driver behaviour.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill invites a larger question: how do we change the system around the driver?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While my suggestions are distinct, they are driven by the same goal: designing safety into the system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A warning symbol is a safer default built into dispensing prescriptions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A Safe Driver Digital Interface Code designs safety into platform apps.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: An annual enforcement report builds accountability into technology and practical tools for small organisations make compliance achievable, so good intentions are not defeated by paperwork.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: None of this dilutes personal responsibility; it strengthens it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A driver supported by clearer information, safer defaults, and better-designed systems is more empowered to do the right thing, and less likely to fail through a moment's inattention.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is the shift before us: not merely to punish the individual after harm occurs, but to design our system so that harm is prevented where possible.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our laws reveal what we refuse to accept.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Over time, through legislation, education and social norms, behaviours that were once common, like driving without seatbelts or holding a phone, became unacceptable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One day, I hope future Singaporeans will look back and wonder why the risks we tolerate today were ever treated as an ordinary part of driving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The best laws do not just punish bad behaviour; they redefine what is acceptable, reshaping our systems so that the safe choice becomes the natural one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The measure of this Bill will not be the number of prosecutions, notices issued or sentence lengths.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Please allow me to address the questions they have raised.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Vikram Nair asked about the gap that a separate offence of purposeful endangerment fills, beyond what is already provided for in the Penal Code today.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I have addressed this in my opening speech.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: He also asked how the Ministry will decide which Act to apply in any given case.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Regarding the offence of purposeful endangerment, Mr Yip Hon Weng asked what would ordinarily amount to the "special reasons" needed to depart from lifetime disqualification, should the offence of purposeful endangerment be made out.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: What constitutes "special reasons" in the context of purposeful endangerment is ultimately to be decided by the Courts.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Courts have, in the context of other traffic offences, found that "special reasons" are extenuating or pressing circumstances and relate to the offence itself and not to the offender.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Yip also asked about how vehicle forfeiture is to be carried out if the vehicle belongs to someone else.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This scenario is provided for under our existing laws.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Wan Rizal noted that clause 6 empowers a District or Magistrate's Court to impose the full penalty, which departs from the usual position under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: He asked about the rationale for this and if the rights of appeal remain fully preserved.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Criminal Procedure Code prescribes the sentencing jurisdiction of the District Court and Magistrate's Court.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, this is subject to any other written law.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Parties may still appeal against the Court's sentencing decision in accordance with the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: To Mr Kenneth Tiong's question on whether his illustrations apply to the purposeful endangerment offence, it will depend on the facts and circumstances of the case.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Regarding the maximum penalties for careless and dangerous driving causing grievous hurt, Dr Wan Rizal asked the Ministry to review, in a few years' time, if this was effective in influencing driver behaviour.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will continue to monitor the road traffic situation closely to ensure that our laws and policies remain adequate.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: That said, we do not expect to see many cases attracting this punishment since the higher maximum penalties should only apply to the most serious forms of grievous hurt.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Choo Pei Ling suggested for permanent and irreversible neurological impairment to be recognised as a distinct aggravating factor in sentencing.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In the context of careless and dangerous driving, the Courts presently recognise three broad factors as aggravating harm factors: first, the nature and location of the injury; second, the degree of permanence of the injury; and third, the impact of the injury on the victim's quality of life.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Courts can consider a victim's neurological impairment in the context of these three factors.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan suggested increasing the maximum penalty for dangerous driving causing death, to narrow the gap with the maximum penalty for purposeful endangerment.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As with other traffic offences, we will continue to review the penalties, including raising the maximum penalties, depending on the road traffic situation.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As we review the penalties in the Act, we will reference penalties in other legislation, such as the Penal Code where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will take the same approach regarding the fines for these offences, as raised by Ms He Ting Ru.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We highlight that generally, the RTA does not allow for the imposition of a fine for more severe forms of driving offences, such as dangerous driving causing death.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In this Bill, we have focused on addressing these egregious forms of driving and therefore, have only reviewed the imprisonment terms for these offences.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Xie has also suggested fully harmonising the maximum penalty for the offence of dangerous driving causing grievous hurt with the offence of dangerous driving causing death.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We have chosen to draw a distinction between death and grievous hurt.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is what the Bill seeks to achieve by increasing the penalties that can be imposed for dangerous driving causing grievous hurt.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Dr Wan Rizal, Dr Choo Pei Ling, Mr Alex Yeo, Mr David Hoe and Mr Andre Low asked about the criminal liability of drivers who take lawfully prescribed or available medication that may impair driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Further, a statutory defence is available for those who can prove two conditions on the balance of probabilities.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: First, that the controlled drug, psychoactive substance or intoxicating substance was lawfully smoked, inhaled, used, consumed or administered.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Second, the individual did not know or have reason to believe that this would affect his or her capacity, at the time of the alleged offence, to have proper control of a motor vehicle.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This addresses Mr Vikram Nair's query regarding occupational or accidental exposure of such substances.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For non-controlled drugs, such as medication, the legal position has not changed.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It continues to be an offence if a person is incapable of having proper control of the vehicle because he or she is impaired by any medicine or other substance.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As for the suggestion to make information on medication-related driving impairment more accessible, the Health Products (Therapeutic Products) Regulations already specifies substances which must come with a label cautioning that they cause drowsiness.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: And if in doubt, members of the public should consult with their healthcare professionals and err on the side of not driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Andre Low asked what constitutes the legal threshold for the new drug driving offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These specified substances comprise controlled drugs, psychoactive substances and intoxicating substances regulated under the three Acts that I have mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Low further asked about analytical thresholds for the new offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The laboratory applies validated analytical limits and reporting criteria when reporting the presence of specified substances in blood.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: These limits are method- and substance-specific and are established to ensure that reported results are reliable, scientifically supportable and thus evidential.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: A concentration below the applicable reporting criteria would not be reported as a positive finding.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Diana Pang and Mr Andre Low asked for more details on the efficacy and reliability of the Handheld Breath Evidential Analyser.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police, with the support of the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, will ensure that the deployed Handheld Breath Evidential Analyser models meet evidential grade standards through testing and certifications in accordance with internationally recognised references, such as the International Organisation of Legal Metrology R126.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Subjects will be shown the test results on the spot.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where it is not practicable to conduct a breath test, the Traffic Police can require the subject to provide a specimen of blood instead.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Pang also asked if the Ministry would consider certifying reliable breath-testing devices for purchase by members of the public, to allow a person who has consumed alcohol to conduct a preliminary self-check before deciding whether to drive.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There is thus no reason to provide breath-testing devices in the market for drivers to self-check their alcohol levels.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The same applies to those who attempt to consume products that claim to help reduce alcohol readings, as drivers should not be drinking in the first place.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Andre Low asked about how the new drink driving thresholds were set and Mr Alex Yeo asked if we had considered a zero-tolerance approach for drink driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: In reviewing the limit, the Ministry considered both the scientific evidence on alcohol-induced impairment and the approaches adopted in comparable jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Scientific evidence shows that impairment begins at low levels of alcohol consumption.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The tightened limit therefore targets the range at which alcohol-induced impairment begins, while also accounting for endogenous alcohol productions where the body naturally produces small amounts of ethanol through normal metabolic processes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As mentioned in my opening speech, I would like to reassure Mr Low that the amendment to the blood authorisation requirement does not diminish the duty of the medical practitioner or nurse to assess whether taking the blood specimen would harm the patient.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: On the contrary, the amended provisions make clear that prior to taking a blood specimen, the medical practitioner or nurse must be satisfied that this will not harm the patient.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying asked if there was evidence to show that accidents resulted from handphone driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: When accidents are reported to the Traffic Police today, there are significant evidential difficulties in proving whether handphone driving contributed to it.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: For one, drivers would not proactively confess that they were in fact using a mobile communication device at the time of the accident.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There is also often no objective video evidence available to establish that a driver was on their mobile communication device at the time of the accident.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: But that does not mean that handphone driving is not dangerous or not prevalent.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Poh Li San asked how the revised handphone driving offence would be enforced.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police intends to leverage technological solutions, such as cameras, as far as possible, to detect and enforce against this offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms Hany Soh sought clarification on the different scenarios that will trigger this offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Lee Hui Ying asked if the Ministry would consider implementing a "one tap" policy for mounted phone use.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Diana Pang asked if an exception can be made for scenarios where the driver's holding of the phone is a split second occurrence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Even in the scenario where the device has fallen from its mount, the driver should stop the vehicle safely before retrieving the device.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: It is dangerous to assume that it is safe to pick up the device while the vehicle is moving, even if just for a second.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: What we are aiming for is a collective change in driver mindset and habits to minimise distractions while on the road.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Several Members raised the issue of increased distractions for drivers, such as use of mounted devices and in-car entertainment systems.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms He Ting Ru asked how the law will address drivers who interact extensively with a mounted device or in-car entertainment system.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: That said, there are existing provisions which target the use of mounted screens in moving vehicles under certain circumstances.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Depending on the facts of the case, for instance, if a driver were to use a mounted device, whether single or multiple, and becomes distracted to the point that it affects his driving behaviour, the driver may be liable for the offence of careless or dangerous driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Rule 126 of the Road Traffic (Motor Vehicles, Construction and Use) Rules already makes it an offence to install any visual display unit in a manner that poses a safety hazard or causes distraction.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will monitor the road traffic situation and we do not preclude making changes to our approach to mounted devices or screens should the need arise.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Dennis Tan asked about the evolving definition of "mobile communication device" and asked about the treatment of wearables.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Under the current section 65B(1A) of the Road Traffic Act, it is not an offence for drivers to drive with wearable devices worn in the manner intended by the manufacturer of the device.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I also thank Mr Tan for his suggestion regarding setting robust vehicle safety standards.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police and LTA will continue to work on this.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Joan Pereira, Ms Hany Soh and Ms Diana Pang compared handphone driving to other behaviours, such as smoking when driving.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The result is that a driver using a handphone while driving has slower reaction times, reduced situational awareness and impaired ability to maintain control of the vehicle.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: That said, we encourage all drivers to free themselves from any distraction while on the roads to protect themselves and others.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Gabriel Lam suggested to take a rehabilitative approach towards first-time offenders and a more punitive approach towards repeat offenders.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Under the Driver Improvement Points System, unless a very serious offence was committed, a first-time offender would generally not have his or her licence suspended immediately.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Hamid Razak asked about safeguards for suspension decisions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The RTA only allows for immediate suspension under limited circumstances, where it is in the interests of public safety to do so.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This power is exercised judiciously only in egregious cases.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The suspension may be rescinded at any time if the investigation reveals that the person was not involved in the commission of any such offence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Neo Kok Beng suggested to immediately suspend the licences of those found to have engaged in deliberate "brake checking".

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such conduct may constitute dangerous driving or purposeful endangerment.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Depending on the facts and circumstances of the case, the driver may also be immediately suspended.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Diana Pang spoke about road hogging, where a driver is in the rightmost lane of the expressway but is not overtaking and has a clear opportunity to switch to a different lane but does not do so, thereby blocking other drivers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: As she noted, the Road Traffic Rules already includes an offence of road hogging and this is enforced by the Traffic Police today.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: MHA and the Traffic Police will consider what more can be done to tackle such behaviour.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I would also like to acknowledge Ms Hazlina Halim's suggestion to scale traffic fines according to income.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This is a complex issue and involves questions of equity and fairness.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We are aware that some jurisdictions have rolled this out and will study their experience.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There will be publicity on mainstream and social media channels, as well as targeted communication through key partners such as NTUC, platform operators and taxi associations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will also update the curriculum in our driving schools to reflect these changes.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Valerie Lee asked if offenders returning to driving after lengthy disqualification can have refresher programmes before their licences are restored.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Today, drivers who are suspended or disqualified from driving for more than one year will have their licences revoked.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Such individuals are encouraged to sign up for refresher driving courses and would have to retake the theory and practical driving tests to obtain a fresh valid driving licence before they can drive again.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Poh Li San suggested ways to better utilise the Road Safety Community Park to educate our children and youths about road safety.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: There are plans to redevelop the Park to cater to a wider range of participants and engage families in road safety education.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We also plan to seek suggestions from stakeholders on how the Park can be made more relevant and engaging.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: More details will be released in due course.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members have asked various questions about the use and limitations of technology for enforcement.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police has been stepping up enforcement, both manual and supported by cameras.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Examples include the Traffic Violation Enforcement Cameras and the switching on of the speeding detection function in our red-light cameras.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will continue to expand our camera-based enforcement efforts, with further details to be shared in due course.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Dr Neo Kok Beng and Ms He Ting Ru also asked about the deployment of cameras to enhance road safety and their effectiveness in targeting speeding respectively.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Overt cameras achieve specific deterrence against speeding in areas where there are higher risks of accidents.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Covert cameras achieve general deterrence and reinforce safe driving behaviour.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar and Ms Hazlina Halim asked about the use of data to identify traffic violation and accident hotspots.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police works closely with LTA to identify locations with high accident rates and develop targeted interventions at these hotspots.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Where a location is identified as a persistent hotspot, it may be designated under LTA's Black Spot programme, a structured initiative to implement more comprehensive traffic engineering measures to address the root causes of accidents at these sites.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police may also step up enforcement at these locations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Valerie Lee asked how many public reports result in warnings, investigations and prosecutions, and if better feedback can be provided to those who submitted evidence.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, due to the volume of submissions, we are presently not able to update every person of the outcome of their feedback.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: We will continue to explore whether it is feasible to do so.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: I would nevertheless like to assure the House that the Traffic Police follows up on all reports received from its online portal, including initiating investigations and acting against violators when a traffic offence is made out.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The remaining reports typically do not disclose sufficient grounds to warrant investigations.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr David Hoe asked if the Traffic Police would publish guidance on the minimum information and evidential quality required for public submissions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police's "Feedback on Road Users" portal already sets out what members of the public should provide when submitting a report, including the date, time and location of the violation, the vehicle registration number and any available evidence such as video or photo.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members of the public are encouraged to refer to these guidelines when making submissions.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police will assess each case on the facts and circumstances submitted.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Regarding automating the issuance of the Notice to Furnish Drivers' Particulars, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Dr Wan Rizal, Dr Hamid Razak, Ms Choo Pei Ling, Mr Vikram Nair, Mr David Hoe and Mr Jackson Lam asked how transparency can be maintained alongside a swift and robust appeal process.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police will consider these suggestions in the development of the automated system.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The legislation provides a permanent safeguard that applications to revoke notices issued through automated processing must be reviewed by an authorised public officer.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Members also had questions on the timelines for appeals.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The Traffic Police aims to resolve appeals submitted by members of the public expeditiously.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: The addressing of appeals will continue to be free of charge.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Those who require assistance with the appeal process can approach their nearest Community Centre or ServiceSG Centre, where staff can help them lodge their appeal digitally.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: However, currently, every traffic violation must be processed by at least one officer.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: This takes considerable time, especially with the significant increase in violations we have seen.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: That said, the automation of enforcement, which this Bill will allow, should expedite the process considerably once we have put in place the necessary systems.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng and Dr Wan Rizal asked if additional administrative guidance or resources can be provided for companies to comply with record-keeping requirements and to monitor if these requirements result in increased costs for platform workers.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: While we understand that such recordkeeping imposes some compliance costs on businesses, we seek the public's understanding that they are necessary to ensure that we can enforce our laws fairly and effectively.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Ms Valerie Lee asked for more information on the limitations of setting up and using traffic cameras for enforcement and plans for upgrading.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Traffic enforcement cameras are typically deployed at locations prone to accidents and traffic violations, subject to space and infrastructure constraints.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Deployment at any given location depends on site conditions such as space availability, power supply and line of sight for the camera to oversee traffic.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
text: Although the changes to Driver Improvement Points System recently announced by the Traffic Police are not part of this Bill, I will address Members' comments as these changes share the same objective of improving safety of our roads.

speaker: Ms Sim Ann
